§How to use this document

This is the long-form companion to the slide deck. It is written to be read in three passes.

  • Pass 1 (30 min). Read §0 and §1. That gives you the whole conceptual frame and the vocabulary — after this you can read any paper in the area without getting lost.
  • Pass 2 (2 h). Add §3 (theory) and §4 (the two big systems). This is where the actual claims live.
  • Pass 3. §5–§7 are the parts people usually skip and then get burned by: what is actually happening inside the loop, what the neighbouring architectures do, and what breaks when you try to serve one of these.

Assumed background: you know what a decoder-only transformer block is (attention + MLP + residual + norm), roughly what KV-caching does, and you have seen chain-of-thought prompting. Nothing else.

If a term is unfamiliar, it is defined. Appendix B explains every complexity class (TC⁰, NC¹, NL, P, "hard", "complete", "uniform", "reduction") and every piece of mathematics used here, from scratch. Appendix C is a one-line glossary of the domain terms. Neither is a prerequisite — follow the links when you hit something.

A note on sources

Every figure is reproduced directly from the paper it is credited to. Claims tagged 2026 preprint come from work posted in 2026 that has had less time to be checked — treat those as directions, not settled facts. Full citations are in §9.

0The question behind it all

Why would anyone run the same weights twice? Because depth is not the same resource as width, and a transformer has a hard ceiling on how much sequential work it can do per token.

0.1 A forward pass is a fixed-size circuit

Take a standard decoder-only transformer with LLL layers. For an input of length nnn, every token's output is produced by a computation graph whose depth is O(L)O(L)O(L) — and crucially, LLL does not depend on nnn. Widening the model (more heads, bigger MLP) makes each layer do more work in parallel; it does not add a single extra sequential step.

This is not a hand-wave; it has a precise complexity-theoretic form. Merrill & Sabharwal (TACL 2023) showed that transformers with logarithmic precision are contained in uniform TC⁰ — the class of problems solvable by constant-depth, polynomial-size threshold circuits. Unpacking that name: Threshold Circuit, and the superscript 0 means the depth does not grow with the input at all. TC⁰ is a very parallel class — everything in it can be done in a constant number of rounds given enough processors.

If the complexity classes are unfamiliar

Read Appendix B.1 — Complexity theory in fifteen minutes now. It defines every class and piece of notation used here (TC⁰, NC¹, NL, P, "hard", "complete", "uniform", "reduction") from scratch, in the order you need them. The one-line version: circuit depth is the number of steps you must do in sequence, and a fixed-depth transformer is a constant-depth circuit.

Problems widely believed to be outside TC⁰ include:

  • Directed graph reachability (is node uuu reachable from node vvv?) — this is NL-complete, where NL is Nondeterministic Logarithmic space, and complete means it is one of the hardest problems in that class.
  • Simulating a finite-state machine for nnn steps — NC¹-hard. NC is Nick's Class (named after Nick Pippenger), and NC¹ is the set of problems solvable by circuits of logarithmic depth; hard means at least as difficult as anything in that class. Some transition compositions can be parallelized, so NC¹ hardness constrains constant-depth threshold-circuit simulation under the relevant class-separation assumptions; it does not prove that every one of n transitions must execute serially.
  • Iterated composition in a non-solvable group — e.g. repeatedly composing permutations of five objects (the group S₅, "symmetric group on 5 elements"). By Barrington's theorem this is the canonical NC¹-complete problem, and it is the formal core of "the model can't do long chains of dependent steps." Non-solvable is a technical property of the group that makes this composition problem NC¹-complete; logarithmic-depth parallel algorithms remain possible; commutative groups like addition mod 2 are solvable and therefore easy.
The one-sentence version

A fixed-depth transformer has a bounded number of architectural stages, but a sequential-looking algorithm is not itself a lower bound on parallel depth. Complexity results constrain specified model families under precision, size, and uniformity assumptions. To claim that a task is beyond a fixed-depth model, use the corresponding formal problem and conditional class separation rather than its most obvious serial algorithm.

This does not imply that addition needs one transformer layer per digit: addition has efficient parallel threshold-circuit algorithms. Nor does widening add arbitrary sequential depth for free. The relevant theoretical distinction is between problem families with known upper bounds or conditional lower bounds under a precise computational model, rather than the apparent number of steps in a human solution.

0.2 Three ways to buy more computation

Given the wall, there are exactly three levers. Keeping them straight is most of the battle.

LeverWhat you addWhat it buysWhat it costs
Parameters
(width, more distinct layers)		More weightsKnowledge capacity. Empirically ≈ 2 bits of memorised fact per parameter — a figure that holds for looped and non-looped models alike (Allen-Zhu & Li; reconfirmed in the Ouro paper).Memory, training FLOPs, serving cost — all permanent.
Tokens
(chain of thought)		More decoding stepsSerial depth and a growing external scratchpad: each emitted token is a full extra pass through the network, and it stays in the context where later tokens can attend to it.Latency scales with tokens; needs CoT training data; context length; everything must be verbalisable.
Depth
(looping / recurrence)		More passes through the same blockSerial depth, decided at inference time, with no extra parameters and no extra tokens.FLOPs per token scale with loop count; state is limited to the fixed-size residual stream; latency is serial and cannot be parallelised.

The reason chain-of-thought works at all, from this angle, is that it is a loop: Feng et al. (2023) and Merrill & Sabharwal (2024) both frame CoT as increasing effective depth by feeding the output back to the input. The Merrill & Sabharwal result is sharp and worth memorising:

No CoT⟶uniform TC0O(log⁡n) CoT steps⟶barely more than TC0O(n) CoT steps⟶within context-sensitive languagespoly⁡(n) CoT steps⟶exactly P\begin{aligned}\text{No CoT}&\longrightarrow\text{uniform }\mathrm{TC}^0\\ O(\log n)\text{ CoT steps}&\longrightarrow\text{barely more than }\mathrm{TC}^0\\ O(n)\text{ CoT steps}&\longrightarrow\text{within context-sensitive languages}\\ \operatorname{poly}(n)\text{ CoT steps}&\longrightarrow\text{exactly }\mathrm P\end{aligned}No CoTO(logn) CoT stepsO(n) CoT stepspoly(n) CoT steps​⟶uniform TC0⟶barely more than TC0⟶within context-sensitive languages⟶exactly P​

Two of those terms may be unfamiliar. P is the class of problems solvable in polynomial time on an ordinary sequential computer — the standard informal meaning of "tractable." The context-sensitive languages are a level of the Chomsky hierarchy (regular ⊂ context-free ⊂ context-sensitive ⊂ recursively enumerable), roughly "recognisable using memory proportional to the input." The result to remember is the last line: a transformer allowed a polynomial number of chain-of-thought steps can compute exactly the problems an ordinary computer can compute in polynomial time. That is a very strong statement, and it is bought entirely with serial steps.

So CoT is a genuine complexity upgrade, and the amount of upgrade is controlled by how long you let the model think. Looping is the same trade made in a different currency.

0.3 Loops vs. CoT: what is really being traded

The naive story — "looping is CoT but in latent space, so it's strictly better" — is wrong, and understanding why is the single most useful thing in this document.

Both mechanisms add serial steps. They differ in what carries state between steps:

  • In CoT, state between steps lives in emitted tokens that accumulate in the context. After mmm steps you have an mmm-token scratchpad that any later step can read. Memory grows with the number of steps.
  • In a compressed loop, state between steps lives in the hidden activations, whose size is fixed by the architecture (n×dn \times dn×d floats, or just ddd per token). Running 100 loops gives you 100 steps of computation but not one extra bit of storage.
The separation

2026 preprint This is formalised as a memory-budget separation: a loop with a compressed recurrent state is a small-space reasoner however long you run it, and under standard complexity assumptions such loops cannot decide problems that are P-complete under logspace reductions — whereas polynomial-length chain-of-thought can. Depth alone does not substitute for a scratchpad.

Reading that phrase: a P-complete problem is one of the hardest in P, and such problems are believed to be inherently sequential — no amount of parallelism collapses them. "Under logspace reductions" names the translation you are allowed to use when comparing two problems: it must itself run in logarithmic space, so it is too weak to do the hard work for you and the comparison stays meaningful. See Appendix B.1 for reductions, hardness and completeness in full.

Pushing in the other direction, Xu & Sato (ICML 2026) prove separations that favour loops: latent thought admits more efficient parallel computation than inherently sequential CoT (a loop updates all nnn positions at once; CoT emits one token at a time), while CoT retains an advantage in stochastic decoding — approximate counting and sampling, which need the randomness of token-level sampling.

And empirically the same trade shows up as a depth–state trade-off: 2026 preprint a minimal Universal Transformer on Sudoku fails at every configuration without learned memory tokens, across seeds, token counts, and both ACT and fixed depth. Looping improves the model's ability to manipulate information; memory determines how much information there is to manipulate. They are complementary resources, not competing ones.

Carry this forward

Loops buy serial depth with parallel updates and constant memory. CoT buys serial depth with a growing scratchpad and stochastic branching. The interesting architectures in §4 and §6 are mostly attempts to get both.

Derivation: separate sequential depth, work, and finite working memory

Resource model. Let the loop hold M scalars of b bits each, so its recurrent state has at most S=Mb bits. The input may be reread through an injection path; explicitly distinguish that read-only input from writable recurrent memory. Each deterministic application of a shared block maps one of at most 2S states to another for the fixed input.

  1. Running r iterations increases sequential computation by r block applications, but it does not increase the number of writable state bits.
  2. If more than 2S steps are taken without halting or receiving new information, some state must repeat by the pigeonhole principle.
  3. Determinism then repeats the entire subsequent trajectory: it enters a cycle. More time cannot create a new independent storage location.
#fixed-memory states≤2MbScratchpad symbol capacity≤mlog⁡2∣V∣ bitsPlus any associated continuous cached states.\begin{aligned}\#\text{fixed-memory states}&\le2^{Mb}\\ \text{Scratchpad symbol capacity}&\le m\log_2|V|\ \mathrm{bits}\\ &\text{Plus any associated continuous cached states.}\end{aligned}#fixed-memory statesScratchpad symbol capacity​≤2Mb≤mlog2​∣V∣ bitsPlus any associated continuous cached states.​

This is a finite-state counting observation, not a proof that all looped language models belong to one particular complexity class. If M grows with input length, so does the bound; unbounded precision, external memory, changing inputs, or injected randomness alter the assumptions. Likewise, a naturally sequential algorithm is not a lower bound: prefix sums and many compositions admit parallel algorithms. Formal TC⁰/NC¹ separations require the stated precision, uniformity, size, and reduction assumptions, and some remain conditional on unproved class separations.

The practical distinction is still useful: extra iterations buy more computation on the available representation, while an expanding CoT or continuous-thought sequence adds addressable history. A fixed-state model may preserve a few crucial facts perfectly and discard others; the counting argument concerns arbitrary independent information, not every long-context task.

Exercise — A cycle is a memory statement, not a reasoning verdict

A deterministic toy loop has 12 bits of writable state and a fixed read-only input. How many distinct states can it visit? If it has run 4,097 transitions without halting, what follows? Does this prove that a real-valued model with unrestricted precision has the same limit?

Show worked solution

There are at most 2¹²=4,096 states. A trajectory containing 4,098 visited states including the initial state must contain a repeat; in fact 4,097 visited states would already suffice. After a repeated state, a deterministic transition on the same fixed input repeats its future, so the trajectory is periodic from some point onward. Unrestricted real precision removes the finite 12-bit state-count premise, so this particular bound does not apply. The result also says nothing about whether a correct answer was already represented before the cycle.

1Anatomy of a looped model

Every paper in this literature is a different setting of the same six knobs. Learn the knobs once and the papers become easy to read.

1.1 The recursion

The minimal looped transformer is three lines:

e=P(x)(embedding / prelude)s0=init(zeros, e, or random noise)st=R(st−1,e),t=1,…,r(shared block)p=C(sr)(coda and LM head)\begin{aligned}e&=P(x)\quad\text{(embedding / prelude)}\\ s_0&=\mathrm{init}\quad\text{(zeros, }e\text{, or random noise)}\\ s_t&=R(s_{t-1},e),\quad t=1,\ldots,r\quad\text{(shared block)}\\ p&=C(s_r)\quad\text{(coda and LM head)}\end{aligned}es0​st​p​=P(x)(embedding / prelude)=init(zeros, e, or random noise)=R(st−1​,e),t=1,…,r(shared block)=C(sr​)(coda and LM head)​

RRR is a stack of kkk ordinary transformer layers. The whole trick is that the same RRR — the same weight matrices — is applied rrr times, so the model has effective depth k⋅rk\cdot rk⋅r with the parameter count of kkk layers. Because rrr is just a loop bound, it can be chosen after training.

1.2 Notation and the two baselines that matter

Saunshi et al.'s notation has become standard and you should adopt it:

k⊗L:k-layer block looped L timesDeffective=kLNparameters≈Nk-layer model\begin{aligned}k\otimes L&:\quad k\text{-layer block looped }L\text{ times}\\ D_{\mathrm{effective}}&=kL\\ N_{\mathrm{parameters}}&\approx N_{k\text{-layer model}}\end{aligned}k⊗LDeffective​Nparameters​​:k-layer block looped L times=kL≈Nk-layer model​​

Any claim about a looped model is meaningless without saying which baseline it is compared against. There are two, and they answer different questions:

BaselineMatched onThe question it answers
(k⊗1)(k \otimes 1)(k⊗1)
iso-param		Parameter count"Did looping give me anything for free?" A looped model should always beat this — otherwise the loop is doing nothing.
(kL⊗1)(kL \otimes 1)(kL⊗1)
iso-FLOP		Compute per token, and effective depth"How much do I lose by tying the weights?" This is the hard comparison: the baseline has LLL× more parameters for the same FLOPs. Matching it means depth, not parameters, was what mattered.

1.3 The six design choices

This table is the reference you will come back to. Every architecture in §4 and §6 is a row-by-row selection from it.

ChoiceOptionsWhy it matters
1. What to loop Whole stack · middle block only · prelude→core→coda Tying the embedding-adjacent layers hurts: the first layers do de-tokenisation and the last do prediction, which are not iterative operations. Middle looping gives better perplexity and more uniform gains than looping everything.
2. Input injection st=R(st−1,e)s_{t} = R(s_{t-1}, e)st​=R(st−1​,e) vs. st=R(st−1)s_{t} = R(s_{t-1})st​=R(st−1​) Input injection supplies the data at every update and is important in the cited empirical recipes. A data-independent autonomous contraction has one input-independent fixed point; however, a larger state can retain the data, and autonomous recurrences need not be globally contractive. Injection is therefore a useful sufficient architectural mechanism, not necessary for every possible data-dependent iterative algorithm.
3. State init Zeros · the embedding eee · random s0∼N(0,σ2I)s_{0} \sim \mathcal N (0, \sigma ^{2}I)s0​∼N(0,σ2I) Random initialization and input injection encourage training a useful iterative operator. Path independence is a property to measure or enforce; those ingredients do not mathematically guarantee convergence to one attractor (§2, §5).
4. Iteration-dependent parameters Fully tied · + step embedding · + per-step norm/LoRA A step embedding (as in the Universal Transformer) lets the block know "which iteration am I on," which helps fit but hurts depth extrapolation — the model learns behaviours specific to an iteration index rather than a repeatable operator.
5. Depth budget Fixed rrr · sampled rrr during training · learned halting Training at one fixed rrr can over-specialize to that depth. Sampling rrr exposes the model to multiple budgets and can improve extrapolation, but neither fixed nor sampled depth determines extrapolation success by itself.
6. Where the loss goes Last step only · every step (deep supervision) · expectation under a learned exit distribution Determines whether intermediate states are meaningful. "Last step only" permits the model to use early iterations as scratch; deep supervision trains intermediate steps to predict useful answers, which can improve early-exit quality without guaranteeing that every intermediate prediction is correct.

1.4 Training a loop

The recursion is a depth-unrolled RNN, and it inherits every RNN training problem.

Memory

Naive backprop through rrr iterations stores activations for all of them: memory is O(r)O(r)O(r), which is exactly what you were trying to avoid. Four escapes, in increasing order of aggression:

  1. Truncated BPTT. Backpropagate through only the last kkk iterations. Memory and backward FLOPs become independent of rrr, so you can afford a heavy-tailed rrr distribution. Huginn fixes k=8k = 8k=8. The prelude receives gradients through injections in the retained differentiable steps; truncation does not restore derivative paths through detached earlier iterations.
  2. Deep supervision. Apply the loss at several points and detach the state between them, so each segment is a short graph. Used by HRM and TRM.
  3. 1-step gradient. Assume the recursion reaches a fixed point and differentiate only the last application — the DEQ trick (§A.1) without the implicit solve. Cheap, and the approximation that TRM's ablation shows is the single most damaging simplification in HRM: 56.5% vs 87.4% on Sudoku-Extreme.
  4. Implicit differentiation. Solve for the fixed point with a root-finder and get the exact gradient with O(1)O(1)O(1) memory (§A.1). Elegant, but needs hyperparameter care and is still unstable at LM scale.

Sampling the depth

To get a model that works at many depths you must train at many depths. Huginn samples rrr per optimiser step from a log-normal Poisson:

τ∼N ⁣(log⁡rˉ−12σ2,σ),σ=12r∼Poisson⁡(eτ)+1\begin{aligned}\tau&\sim\mathcal N\!\left(\log\bar r-\frac12\sigma^2,\sigma\right),\quad\sigma=\frac12\\ r&\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(e^\tau)+1\end{aligned}τr​∼N(logrˉ−21​σ2,σ),σ=21​∼Poisson(eτ)+1​

With target mean recurrence rˉ=32\bar r=32rˉ=32 this gives mean 33, median 29, mode 24 — i.e. most steps are cheaper than the mean, with a heavy tail of occasional very deep steps. That tail is what teaches the model to keep improving past its typical budget; the truncated BPTT is what makes the tail affordable.

Stability

Two failure modes recur across every paper here:

  • The loop learns to ignore its state. Huginn's ablation runs found a local minimum where the model early-on learns to ignore the incoming state sss, after which validation perplexity is identical at r=1r = 1r=1 and r=32r = 32r=32. The model trained fine; it just wasn't a recurrent model any more. Always check that perplexity improves with rrr — that is the only real test.
  • Halting collapse. Any learned exit gate is prone to collapsing to one depth. Ouro's analysis is the clearest: as the exit distribution concentrates on late steps, those steps get more training signal, their loss drops, which pulls even more mass to the end — a self-reinforcing collapse onto t=Tmax⁡t = T_{\max}t=Tmax​. The fix is an entropy bonus (§4.2). 2026 preprint In ACT-style halting the symmetric failure is a "shallow halt equilibrium"; inverting the halting bias to −3 ("deep start") reportedly removes it.

Derivation: derive the full shared-weight gradient and what truncation removes

Column-vector convention. Let st=Rθ(st−1,e), with terminal loss ℓ(sr). Define Jt=∂st/∂st−1 and Bt=∂Rθ(st−1,e)/∂θ, the direct parameter derivative holding the incoming state fixed. Assume s₀ is independent of θ for the displayed formula.

  1. Differentiate one recurrence: dst/dθ=Jt dst−1/dθ+Bt.
  2. Substitute repeatedly. Each use of the shared θ contributes once, propagated through every later state Jacobian.
  3. Contract the final state derivative with ∇s_rℓ.
dsrdθ=∑t=1rJrJr−1⋯Jt+1Bt∇θℓ=∑t=1rBt⊤Jt+1⊤⋯Jr⊤∇srℓ\begin{aligned}\frac{ds_r}{d\theta}&=\sum_{t=1}^rJ_rJ_{r-1}\cdots J_{t+1}B_t\\ \nabla_\theta\ell&=\sum_{t=1}^rB_t^\top J_{t+1}^\top\cdots J_r^\top\nabla_{s_r}\ell\end{aligned}dθdsr​​∇θ​ℓ​=t=1∑r​Jr​Jr−1​⋯Jt+1​Bt​=t=1∑r​Bt⊤​Jt+1⊤​⋯Jr⊤​∇sr​​ℓ​

An empty Jacobian product is I for t=r. Truncating to the last K iterations keeps only t≥r−K+1 and treats sr−K as a constant. This is generally a biased gradient of the full unrolled objective, even though the forward trajectory still used r steps. If ‖Jt‖≤ρ<1 and ‖Btᵀ…‖ is bounded via ‖Bt‖‖∇ℓ‖≤C, the omitted gradient norm is at most C∑j=Kr−1ρj≤CρK1−ρC\sum_{j=K}^{r-1}\rho^j\le\frac{C\rho^K}{1-\rho}C∑j=Kr−1​ρj≤1−ρCρK​. Without contraction that guarantee disappears.

Input injection gives the prelude a direct derivative through each retained differentiable iteration. It does not recover paths deliberately detached or executed without gradient tracking. Sampling forward depth and fixing K therefore changes both compute and gradient bias. With Huginn’s Poisson-lognormal schedule, if τ∼N(log r̄−σ²/2,σ²), λ=eτ, and r=1+Poisson(λ), then E[r]=1+r̄ and Var(r)=r̄+r̄²(eσ²−1). This follows from E[λ]=r̄ and the law of total variance, and explains why average depth alone understates training-step variability.

Exercise — Measure truncation bias in a scalar recurrence

Let sₜ=a sₜ₋₁+θ, s₀=0, a=0.5, r=4, and loss ℓ=s₄. Find dℓ/dθ exactly and using only the last K=2 steps. Verify the contraction bound with C=1.

Show worked solution

The exact derivative is 1+a+a²+a³=1+0.5+0.25+0.125=1.875. The last-two-step gradient is 1+a=1.5. Omitted contribution is 0.375. The finite-tail sum a²+a³ is exactly 0.375, while the infinite-tail upper bound ρᴷ/(1−ρ)=0.25/0.5=0.5 is valid but looser. The forward value s₄ has not changed; only the differentiated paths have changed.

1.5 Inference and halting

Once trained with variable depth, you have four ways to pick rrr at inference:

StrategyHowUsed by
Fixed budgetSet rrr globally per query. Simple, batches perfectly.Ouro releases (R=4R = 4R=4); most evaluations
ACT haltingPer token, a unit emits a halting probability each step; stop when the cumulative sum exceeds 1−ε1 - \varepsilon 1−ε; add a "ponder cost" to the loss to discourage thinking forever.Universal Transformer; PonderNet
Convergence testStop when the output distribution stops moving: exit when KL⁡(pt∥pt−1)<5⋅10−4\operatorname{KL}(p_{t} \| p_{t-1}) < 5\cdot 10^{-4}KL(pt​∥pt−1​)<5⋅10−4. Requires no extra parameters and no training — it is available zero-shot.Huginn
Learned exit gateA small head predicts an exit probability ptp_{t}pt​ per step; exit when the CDF crosses a threshold. Trained jointly with the LM loss.Ouro / LoopLM; MoR (per-token routing)
The KV-cache problem with early exit

If token iii exits at depth 8 while token i+1i+1i+1 reaches depth 20, per-depth KV entries for token iii at depths 9–20 were never computed. One policy substitutes the deepest available entry. Shared K,V projections make the entries compatible in shape and coordinate convention, but different hidden states generally produce different K,V values. This is an approximation to full per-depth caching, supported by empirical evaluation rather than an exactness consequence of tied weights.

Two more inference-time perks fall out of recurrence almost for free: self-speculative decoding (use the output at a shallow depth as the draft, the deep output as the verifier — one model, no draft model needed), and zero-shot KV-cache sharing across recurrence steps to cut memory.

A subtler one: Huginn can warm-start the next token's s0s_{0}s0​ from the previous token's converged state instead of fresh noise — a "zero-shot continuous chain-of-thought." On MMLU categories this reduces the mean number of steps to convergence (e.g. philosophy: 14.6 → 13.5), because the model reuses the latent work it already did.

Derivation: distinguish ACT remainder weights from a stochastic halting law

Hazard formulation. Let ht∈[0,1] be the probability of stopping at step t conditional on reaching it. Define survival S0=1 and St=∏j≤t(1−hj). Then pt=htSt−1=St−1−St. Force hT=1 at a finite cap to absorb all remaining probability.

  1. Summing pt telescopes to 1−ST=1.
  2. Write the stopping depth as τ=Σt=1..T1[τ≥t].
  3. Take expectation: E[τ]=Σt=1..TP(τ≥t)=Σt=1..TSt−1.
(h1,h2,h3)=(0.4,0.4,1)(p1,p2,p3)=(0.4,0.24,0.36)E[τ]=1+0.6+0.36=1.96=1⋅0.4+2⋅0.24+3⋅0.36\begin{aligned}(h_1,h_2,h_3)&=(0.4,0.4,1)\\ (p_1,p_2,p_3)&=(0.4,0.24,0.36)\\ \mathbb E[\tau]&=1+0.6+0.36=1.96\\ &=1\cdot0.4+2\cdot0.24+3\cdot0.36\end{aligned}(h1​,h2​,h3​)(p1​,p2​,p3​)E[τ]​=(0.4,0.4,1)=(0.4,0.24,0.36)=1+0.6+0.36=1.96=1⋅0.4+2⋅0.24+3⋅0.36​

ACT’s original mechanism is different. It accumulates emitted halting scores until their sum reaches 1−ε, then uses a final remainder R=1−Σt<Nht as the final mixture weight. With scores (0.4,0.4,0.4) and threshold 0.99, it takes N=3 steps and uses weights (0.4,0.4,0.2), not (0.4,0.24,0.36). Its ponder penalty N+R is 3.2, distinct from both the executed count N and the mixture-weighted mean depth 1.8. PonderNet’s hazard distribution and geometric prior make a probabilistic stopping interpretation explicit. Keep those semantics separate when deriving expected compute.

Exercise — Compute survival before computing the expected budget

A capped hazard model has h=(0.2,0.5,1). Compute its stop probabilities and expected depth two ways. If each loop costs 3 ms and fixed prelude/coda cost is 2 ms, what is its expected serial latency under this constant-cost toy model?

Show worked solution

Survivals before each step are 1,0.8,0.4, so p=(0.2,0.4,0.4). Weighted mean is 1·0.2+2·0.4+3·0.4=2.2; the survival sum is 1+0.8+0.4=2.2. Expected latency is 2+3·2.2=8.6 ms. A GPU batch with different exit depths may not realize that mean because kernels can run until the deepest active item exits.

1.6 The cost model

Worth internalising before you get excited about "3.5B parameters performing like 50B."

Nparams∝k(constant in r)Ftoken=rkFlayerMKV∝rk(unless shared)Critical path=r sequential block applications\begin{aligned}N_{\mathrm{params}}&\propto k\quad\text{(constant in }r\text{)}\\ F_{\mathrm{token}}&=rkF_{\mathrm{layer}}\\ M_{\mathrm{KV}}&\propto rk\quad\text{(unless shared)}\\ \text{Critical path}&=r\text{ sequential block applications}\end{aligned}Nparams​Ftoken​MKV​Critical path​∝k(constant in r)=rkFlayer​∝rk(unless shared)=r sequential block applications​

So a looped model with r=32r = 32r=32 is not cheap. What it is, is small: it has the memory footprint of a small model and the compute profile of a large one. That trade is attractive exactly when weights are the bottleneck (edge deployment, memory-bound serving) and unattractive when FLOPs or latency are.

Comparison worth keeping straight

CoT and looping both cost extra forward passes. The difference is granularity: CoT does one full-depth pass per emitted token and the cache grows with tokens; looping does rrr block-passes per token position, all positions updated in parallel, and the cache grows with rrr. For a 200-token CoT you pay 200 full-model passes serially. For r=32r = 32r=32 looping you pay 32 block-passes — but you also never get the 200-token scratchpad.

2Where this came from

Problems defining this stage. The foundational work separates three questions often conflated in recurrent models: whether weights can be shared across depth, whether computation can stop adaptively, and whether the final representation can be defined as an equilibrium. These choices change different parts of training, memory use and inference.

None of this is new. What is new is the motivation: the 2018 papers looped for parameter efficiency, the 2025 papers loop for reasoning. Knowing the ancestry saves you from re-deriving solved problems.

Universal Transformer (Dehghani et al., ICLR 2019)

Core idea. Apply the same transformation repeatedly across depth, optionally with adaptive computation time at each position. This makes iterative refinement and shared parameters explicit architectural choices.

One shared block applied TTT times over depth, with a per-position Adaptive Computation Time halting mechanism so different tokens can think for different numbers of steps. Under the standard idealisations (unbounded steps, unbounded precision) it is Turing-complete, unlike the vanilla transformer. It beat LSTMs and vanilla transformers on bAbI and algorithmic tasks and set state of the art on LAMBADA — and then the field went and scaled parameters instead for six years.

ACT (Graves 2016) and PonderNet (Banino et al. 2021)

Core idea. ACT forms a weighted output from successive states using a learned halting signal and a remainder weight; PonderNet learns a probabilistic halting distribution. Both allocate computation adaptively, but their halting laws and objectives are distinct.

The halting machinery UT borrowed. ACT accumulates a halting probability per step and stops when it crosses 1−ε1 - \varepsilon 1−ε, with a "ponder cost" penalty on total steps. PonderNet reframes this as a proper probability distribution over halting steps, trained with a KL term toward a geometric prior — cleaner gradients, less hyperparameter sensitivity. Every learned-exit scheme you will meet in §4 is a descendant of one of these two.

ALBERT (Lan et al., ICLR 2020)

Core idea. Share parameters across transformer layers to reduce stored model size. Parameter sharing establishes a useful baseline for recurrence, but does not itself make the number of inference iterations adaptive.

Cross-layer parameter sharing in BERT, purely for parameter efficiency. Important as the counterexample: ALBERT shares weights but does not vary depth at inference and makes no reasoning claim. Sharing weights and using recurrence as compute are separable ideas; ALBERT did only the first.

Deep Equilibrium Models (Bai, Kolter & Koltun, NeurIPS 2019)

Core idea. Define the representation as a fixed point of a shared transformation and differentiate through that equilibrium implicitly. The method replaces explicit storage of a long unrolled graph with root-finding and a corresponding backward linear-system problem.

Take the loop to its limit: instead of running rrr steps, solve directly for the fixed point z∗=f(z∗,x)z^* = f(z^*, x)z∗=f(z∗,x) with a root-finder, and get gradients by implicit differentiation with O(1)O(1)O(1) memory (derivation in §A.1). DEQs are the theoretical ceiling of this whole family — "infinite depth, constant memory" — and the source of the fixed-point language everyone else uses.

Deep thinking networks (Schwarzschild et al. 2021; Bansal et al., NeurIPS 2022)

Core idea. Train shared recurrent computation to iteratively refine a solution and investigate whether additional test-time iterations improve it. The important question is whether the learned dynamics continue solving the task beyond the training unroll.

The most underrated papers in the lineage, and the ones that discovered the failure mode you will hit first. Train a recurrent convnet on small mazes, run it longer at test time, and it solves larger ones — logical extrapolation. But run it much longer and behaviour degrades: they named this overthinking. Two fixes, both of which reappear in the 2025 LM papers under different names:

  • Recall — keep an explicit copy of the problem in memory so it cannot be forgotten. This is exactly what "input injection" is in §1.3.
  • Progressive training — randomise the iteration count so the model learns a repeatable operator rather than iteration-index-specific behaviour. This is exactly Huginn's sampled rrr.

With both, a network trained on 9×9 mazes solves 201×201 mazes without retraining — some runs equivalent to over 100,000 convolutional layers.

Path independence (Anil et al., NeurIPS 2022)

Core idea. Encourage recurrent computation to approach a useful result independently of its starting state. This distinguishes a robust iterative solver from a network that depends on following one particular finite training trajectory.

The mechanistic explanation for why those fixes work. A system is path independent if it converges to the same attractor regardless of initialisation, given enough compute. Anil et al. found that path independence strongly correlates with generalising to harder instances — and then, because correlation could be confounded, intervened: regularisers that promote path independence improve generalisation, regularisers that suppress it hurt. For a trained equilibrium model, per-example path independence on OOD inputs predicts per-example accuracy.

Diagnostic you can run today

Run the same input from several initial states and measure both state separation and output quality over depth. Convergence across initializations is evidence consistent with path independence; persistent separation or cycles warrant investigation. Neither outcome alone proves whether a learned model will extrapolate or reason correctly. Compare this diagnostic with task accuracy and sensitivity to interventions.

3Theory: what looping actually buys

Problems defining this stage. The theoretical stage asks what additional sequential computation shared weights can express and learn. Simulation constructions and iterative-algorithm examples clarify possible expressivity, but their memory, width and convergence assumptions must be kept separate from practical parameter savings.

Three families of result — constructions (what a loop can express), learning results (what a loop does learn), and separations (what a loop cannot do). Read them in that order.

Derivation: derive implicit differentiation and the one-step approximation error

Fixed point. Let s*=Rθ(s*,e), with differentiable R, and assume I−J is invertible at the solution, where J=∂R/∂s. Holding e fixed for clarity, differentiate both sides with respect to θ. The dependence of s* on θ occurs both inside R’s state input and directly through its parameters:

ds∗dθ=Jds∗dθ+B,B=∂R∂θ(I−J)ds∗dθ=Bg=∇s∗ℓ,(I−J⊤)v=g∇θℓ=B⊤v+direct loss derivative\begin{aligned}\frac{ds^*}{d\theta}&=J\frac{ds^*}{d\theta}+B,\quad B=\frac{\partial R}{\partial\theta}\\ (I-J)\frac{ds^*}{d\theta}&=B\\ g&=\nabla_{s^*}\ell,\quad(I-J^\top)v=g\\ \nabla_\theta\ell&=B^\top v+\text{direct loss derivative}\end{aligned}dθds∗​(I−J)dθds∗​g∇θ​ℓ​=Jdθds∗​+B,B=∂θ∂R​=B=∇s∗​ℓ,(I−J⊤)v=g=B⊤v+direct loss derivative​

This avoids explicitly storing every forward iterate, but requires finding a suitable fixed point and solving a linear adjoint system. It is not zero compute or zero solver memory. A sufficient condition for a Neumann-series solution is ‖J‖<1, giving v=Σj≥0(Jᵀ)jg. Invertibility can hold without this norm condition; then that particular series need not converge.

A one-step gradient uses v≈g and drops every Jᵀg term. With ‖J‖≤ρ<1, the omitted adjoint has norm at most ρ‖g‖/(1−ρ). For the scalar fixed point s*=a s*+θ, exact ds*/dθ=1/(1−a), whereas the one-step approximation is 1. At a=0.9 these are 10 and 1. This is why “the state converged” alone does not justify a one-step gradient: convergence can be slow, leaving a large inverse-Jacobian amplification.

3.1 A looped transformer is a programmable computer

Core idea. Construct attention and feed-forward operations that manipulate an explicit memory and instruction state across repeated applications. The construction demonstrates programmable sequential computation under the stated resource assumptions.

Giannou, Rajput, Sohn, Lee, Lee & Papailiopoulos (ICML 2023) asked the maximal version of the question: not "is a loop useful" but "how much of a computer is it?"

The construction reverse-engineers attention into primitive computing blocks — lexicographic comparison, pointer arithmetic, conditional branching, function calls, a program counter — and then builds a one-instruction set computer on top. The instruction is SUBLEQ:

They then generalise it to FLEQ, where the subtraction is replaced by any of a predefined set of functions hard-coded into the weights:

mem[c] = f_m( mem[a], mem[b] )
if mem[flag] ≤ 0:  goto instruction p

With fmf_mfm​ allowed to be matrix multiplication or a non-linearity, one "instruction" does real work, so iterative algorithms compile to short programs.

Theorem 1 (informal)

There exists a looped transformer with fewer than 13 layers that emulates a general-purpose computer: a basic calculator, a linear-algebra library (transpose, multiplication, approximate inverse, power iteration), and in-context learning algorithms including SGD with backpropagation on an implicit neural network. Width is typically O(log⁡(input length)+d)O(\log(\text{input length}) + d)O(log(input length)+d).

The crucial structural point: the depth required does not depend on the length of the program. A 13-layer network can run a 10,000-line program, because program length turns into loop iterations, not layers. Without the loop you would need depth proportional to the program.

What this does not say

The weights are hand-constructed, not learned. Nothing here says gradient descent would ever find such a solution, or that this is an efficient way to compute anything — the authors say so themselves. Read it as an expressivity upper bound: the architecture is not the limitation. What §3.2 adds is evidence that training actually reaches useful points in that space.

3.2 Loops learn iterative algorithms

Core idea. Use repeated shared updates to emulate an iterative algorithm such as gradient descent for in-context regression. Each iteration applies the same update rule, so convergence depends on the learned step size and the problem’s spectrum.

The cleanest empirical handle is in-context linear regression. Feed a prompt (x1,y1,…,xk,yk,xtest)(x_{1}, y_{1}, \ldots , x_k, y_k, x_{\mathrm{test}})(x1​,y1​,…,xk​,yk​,xtest​) with yi=w⊤xiy_{i} = w^\top x_{i}yi​=w⊤xi​ and ask the model to predict ytesty_{\mathrm{test}}ytest​. There are two ways to solve it:

w^=(X⊤X)−1X⊤y(matrix inverse)wt+1=wt−ηX⊤(Xwt−y)(iterative update)\begin{aligned}\widehat w&=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y\quad\text{(matrix inverse)}\\ w_{t+1}&=w_t-\eta X^\top(Xw_t-y)\quad\text{(iterative update)}\end{aligned}wwt+1​​=(X⊤X)−1X⊤y(matrix inverse)=wt​−ηX⊤(Xwt​−y)(iterative update)​

Details worth knowing from that paper:

  • Input injection matters in the reported ablation. Removing it led the studied looped model to diverge beyond its trained horizon. This is evidence about that architecture and training setup, not an impossibility theorem for every state-only recurrence.
  • The loop schedule matters. Training samples iteration counts from a window [b,b+T][b, b+T][b,b+T]; too small a bbb makes the model diverge past the trained horizon. This is the same lesson as "progressive training" from §2, rediscovered.
  • It learns an algorithm, not the algorithm. Shift the test distribution of xxx (e.g. sample x=3zx = 3zx=3z, z∼N(0,I)z \sim \mathcal N (0,I)z∼N(0,I)) and it degrades. It has internalised a procedure that is correct on the training distribution, not the distribution-free least-squares solver.

On the theory side, Gatmiry, Saunshi, Reddi, Jegelka & Kumar (ICML 2024) close the loop: looped transformers provably learn to implement multi-step preconditioned gradient descent for in-context learning. So for this task family the story is complete — the construction exists, training finds it, and we can prove training finds it.

Derivation: derive when a repeated gradient step converges and why scale shift breaks it

In-context least squares. Let X∈ℝn×d, y∈ℝn, and F(w)=½‖Xw−y‖². Write H=XᵀX and b=Xᵀy. The gradient is Hw−b, so a fixed-step loop is wt+1=(I−ηH)wt+ηb. Assume H is positive definite for a unique minimizer w*=H⁻¹b.

  1. Subtract the fixed-point equation w*=(I−ηH)w*+ηb to get et+1=(I−ηH)et.
  2. Diagonalize symmetric H=UΛUᵀ. Each eigen-coordinate follows et+1,j=(1−ηλj)et,j.
  3. Every coordinate contracts exactly when |1−ηλj|<1, so 0<η<2/λmax.
∥et∥2≤ρt∥e0∥2,ρ=max⁡j∣1−ηλj∣<1η=2λmax⁡+λmin⁡ρ=κ−1κ+1,κ=λmax⁡λmin⁡\begin{aligned}\|e_t\|_2&\le\rho^t\|e_0\|_2,\quad\rho=\max_j|1-\eta\lambda_j|<1\\ \eta&=\frac2{\lambda_{\max}+\lambda_{\min}}\\ \rho&=\frac{\kappa-1}{\kappa+1},\quad\kappa=\frac{\lambda_{\max}}{\lambda_{\min}}\end{aligned}∥et​∥2​ηρ​≤ρt∥e0​∥2​,ρ=jmax​∣1−ηλj​∣<1=λmax​+λmin​2​=κ+1κ−1​,κ=λmin​λmax​​​

A loop can learn an update resembling this iteration, but empirical convergence alone does not identify the exact optimizer. If inputs scale to X′=3X, then H′=9H. A formerly stable η may become unstable unless it adapts; the safe upper bound shrinks by nine. If H is singular, components in its nullspace are not contracted, and convergence/uniqueness need a different statement. Preconditioning changes the effective spectrum and can improve convergence.

Data access matters because the update uses H and b each step. Reinjecting e is one way to supply them. It is not mathematically the only way: a larger recurrent state could retain H,b or an equivalent representation and implement the same update autonomously. The empirical benefit of input injection should be interpreted as a useful architectural constraint, not a universal impossibility theorem for every recurrence without an explicit injection edge.

Exercise — Check a learned iteration under feature rescaling

H has eigenvalues 1 and 4, and η=0.4. Compute the two error multipliers and the contraction factor. Then scale X by 3 while keeping η fixed. Give a stable replacement step size and its resulting multipliers.

Show worked solution

Initially the multipliers are 1−0.4·1=0.6 and 1−0.4·4=−0.6, so ρ=0.6. After scaling, eigenvalues are 9 and 36; fixed η gives −2.6 and −13.4, both unstable. Dividing η by nine gives η′=0.4/9≈0.044444, restoring multipliers 0.6 and −0.6. This illustrates a specific spectrum shift; a trained model may learn adaptive preconditioning, so the example is not a theorem that all looped models fail under rescaling.

3.3 Latent thoughts: depth without parameters

Core idea. Study looped transformers as parallel latent computation over existing token positions, with constructions relating recurrent depth to ordinary depth and chain-of-thought. Matched-budget experiments then separate reasoning benefits from the memorization capacity of additional independent weights.

Saunshi et al. (ICLR 2025) is the paper that connected looping to reasoning rather than to efficiency. Their framing claim:

Claim 1

Many reasoning problems require large depth but not necessarily many parameters — so they can be solved by looped models.

The two theorems

Theorem 1 (a loop can simulate depth). Any transformer with LLL layers, embedding size ddd and hidden size dFFd_{\mathrm{FF}}dFF​ can be simulated by a 1-layer transformer looped LLL times, with embedding size d+Ld + Ld+L and hidden size L⋅dFFL\cdot d_{\mathrm{FF}}L⋅dFF​. Read the overhead carefully: the extra LLL embedding dimensions act as a step counter, and the FF blow-up stores all LLL layers' worth of weights in one layer. It is a simulation result, not a compression result — but it shows the looped architecture class is not expressively weaker.

Theorem 2 (a loop can simulate CoT). Any LLL-layer transformer on an nnn-length input generating mmm CoT tokens can be simulated by a looped model with L+O(1)L + O(1)L+O(1) distinct layers and O(log⁡(n+m))O(\log(n+m))O(log(n+m)) extra embedding size. The intuition is the heart of the paper:

Latent thoughts

Chain-of-thought is a looped model — one that emits exactly one thought token per iteration. A looped transformer is more general because each iteration produces a latent update at every position at once: nnn "latent thoughts" per loop instead of one. That is the parallelism advantage that Xu & Sato later make formal (§0.3).

They also give near-optimal constructions for group composition (generalising multi-digit addition) and the ppp-hop induction problem, the latter with a one-layer looped transformer.

The empirical results, and the surprise

Three findings to take away:

  1. On synthetic reasoning, k⊗L≈kL⊗1k\otimes L \approx kL\otimes 1k⊗L≈kL⊗1. On addition, ppp-hop induction and symbolic grade-school math, a looped model nearly matches the iso-FLOP baseline and vastly beats the iso-param one.
  2. On real language models: worse perplexity, better reasoning. This is the counter-intuitive part. Looped LMs lose on validation perplexity to the iso-FLOP baseline (perplexity depends strongly on parameter count) yet win on downstream reasoning at equal perplexity. Looping is an inductive bias, not just compression.
  3. There is a depth scaling law. Accuracy fits Acc⁡≈αlog⁡D+β\operatorname{Acc}\approx\alpha\log D+\betaAcc≈αlogD+β in effective depth DDD, for both looped and non-looped models. Comparing slopes, αloopαbase\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{loop}}}{\alpha_{\mathrm{base}}}αbase​αloop​​ ≈ 0.5 for memorisation tasks but reaches 1.2 for reasoning primitives — on those tasks a loop is worth more than an equal number of fresh parameters.

The practical spin-off

If looping is a useful inductive bias, can you get it without paying for it? Their answer: keep a full non-looped LLL-layer model but add a regulariser pulling the weights of every kkk-layer block toward each other (toward their mean), with strength λreg\lambda _{\mathrm{reg}}λreg​. The model keeps free parameters for perplexity while inheriting the bias. At k=4,λreg=10k = 4, \lambda _{\mathrm{reg}} = 10k=4,λreg​=10 on a 24-layer 1B model: perplexity 7.38 vs 7.40 baseline (neutral), math word problems 36.4 vs 29.3, reasoning primitives 57.2 vs 47.5. This is the cheapest idea in the whole literature to try on an existing training run.

Derivation: derive what soft weight tying does to the training gradient

One corresponding matrix across m blocks. Let W₁,…,Wm be same-shaped weights and W̄=m⁻¹ΣWj. Define a sharing regularizer R=λ2∑j∥Wj−Wˉ∥F2R=\frac\lambda2\sum_j\|W_j-\bar W\|_F^2R=2λ​∑j​∥Wj​−Wˉ∥F2​. Expand the squared norms to separate individual weights from their mean:

∑j∥Wj−Wˉ∥2=∑j∥Wj∥2−m∥Wˉ∥2=1m∑i<j∥Wi−Wj∥2∂R∂Wi=λ(Wi−Wˉ)\begin{aligned}\sum_j\|W_j-\bar W\|^2&=\sum_j\|W_j\|^2-m\|\bar W\|^2\\ &=\frac1m\sum_{i<j}\|W_i-W_j\|^2\\ \frac{\partial R}{\partial W_i}&=\lambda(W_i-\bar W)\end{aligned}j∑​∥Wj​−Wˉ∥2∂Wi​∂R​​=j∑​∥Wj​∥2−m∥Wˉ∥2=m1​i<j∑​∥Wi​−Wj​∥2=λ(Wi​−Wˉ)​

The derivative through W̄ matters, but cancels because Σ(Wj−W̄)=0. A gradient step of size η changes Wi to Wi−ηλ(Wi−W̄), ignoring task loss. Summing over i leaves the mean unchanged. For 0≤ηλ≤1, each matrix moves a convex fraction toward that mean, and deviations shrink by 1−ηλ.

This explains how soft tying promotes similar transformations while retaining separate parameters for task learning. It does not reduce the number of stored matrices or forward-pass FLOPs by itself. Even if the matrices become close, replacing them by one shared matrix is an additional approximation requiring evaluation. The reported reasoning gains are empirical evidence for an inductive bias; the gradient identity does not prove that reasoning must improve or perplexity must remain unchanged.

3.4 Where loops fall short

To keep the picture honest, collect the negative results in one place:

ResultWhat it says
Memory-budget separation
2026 preprint		A compressed loop has a fixed-size recurrent state, so it remains a small-space reasoner no matter how long it runs. Under standard assumptions it cannot decide problems P-complete under logspace reductions; polynomial-length CoT can. Depth is not a substitute for a scratchpad.
CoT keeps stochastic decoding
(Xu & Sato, ICML 2026)		Token sampling gives CoT approximate counting and sampling abilities that deterministic latent iteration does not have.
UTs need memory
2026 preprint		Empirically, a minimal single-block UT with ACT solves Sudoku-Extreme only when given learned memory tokens — no configuration without them reached non-trivial performance. Working-memory bandwidth and computational depth are complementary resources.
Learned ≠ general
(Yang et al. 2024)		Looped in-context learners break under input-distribution shift: they learn a procedure tuned to the training distribution, not the underlying algorithm.
Simulation overheads are real
(Saunshi et al. 2025)		The "1 layer looped LLL times simulates LLL layers" result needs L⋅dFFL\cdot d_{\mathrm{FF}}L⋅dFF​ hidden width. Looping does not make parameters disappear; it moves them.

4Practice: two systems at scale

Problems defining this stage. Scaling recurrence to language models requires stable long unrolls, affordable gradients and a training distribution over depths. The central empirical question is whether extra loop iterations improve useful predictions at a fixed parameter or compute budget, rather than simply increasing latency.

Two teams took the idea to real pre-training budgets from opposite ends. Huginn maximises depth and keeps halting training-free; Ouro keeps depth modest and learns where to stop. Reading both is the fastest way to see which choices are load-bearing.

4.1 Huginn-3.5B — recurrent depth (Geiping et al., 2025)

Core idea. Use a prelude, a repeatedly applied shared core with input injection, and a coda, training across sampled recurrence depths. Truncated backpropagation controls training memory while repeated core applications provide an adjustable inference-compute budget.

The bet: make depth the primary test-time knob and push rrr as high as possible. 3.5B parameters, 800B tokens, trained on Frontier.

Architecture

ComponentSetting
Block layout(prelude, core, coda) = (2, 4, 2) transformer layers
Parameter split1.5B prelude+coda · 1.5B in the recurrent core · 0.5B tied embeddings
Widthh=5280h = 5280h=5280; 55 heads × 96; MLP inner dim 17920
Layer internalsCausal self-attention with RoPE (base 50000), gated SiLU MLP, RMSNorm (ε=10−6\varepsilon = 10^{-6}ε=10−6), learnable biases on queries and keys only
Normalisation"Sandwich" ordering — a norm before and after each sub-layer, specifically to stabilise the recurrence
OptimiserAdam with decoupled weight decay, β=(0.9,0.95)\beta = (0.9, 0.95)β=(0.9,0.95), η=5⋅10−4\eta = 5\cdot 10^{-4}η=5⋅10−4, update clipping, grad clip 1.0, 4096-step warmup then constant LR
e=P(x),s0∼N(0,σ2Inh)si=R(e,si−1),i=1,…,rp=C(sr)x^ℓ=n2 ⁣(xℓ−1+Attn⁡(n1(xℓ−1)))xℓ=n4 ⁣(x^ℓ+MLP⁡(n3(x^ℓ)))\begin{aligned}e&=P(x),\quad s_0\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2I_{nh})\\ s_i&=R(e,s_{i-1}),\quad i=1,\ldots,r\\ p&=C(s_r)\\ \widehat x_\ell&=n_2\!\left(x_{\ell-1}+\operatorname{Attn}(n_1(x_{\ell-1}))\right)\\ x_\ell&=n_4\!\left(\widehat x_\ell+\operatorname{MLP}(n_3(\widehat x_\ell))\right)\end{aligned}esi​pxℓ​xℓ​​=P(x),s0​∼N(0,σ2Inh​)=R(e,si−1​),i=1,…,r=C(sr​)=n2​(xℓ−1​+Attn(n1​(xℓ−1​)))=n4​(xℓ​+MLP(n3​(xℓ​)))​

Note the two deliberate choices from §1.3: random s0s_{0}s0​ (for path independence) and input injection of eee at every step (so the operator is a function of the data, and so the prelude receives gradients even under truncated BPTT).

Training

rˉ=32\bar r=32rˉ=32, sampled per step from the log-normal Poisson of §1.4 (mean 33, median 29, mode 24); truncated BPTT through the last k=8k = 8k=8 iterations. Note a systems detail that matters at scale: rrr is sampled the same across data-parallel workers, otherwise workers idle waiting for whichever one drew the largest rrr.

The failure runs are the most useful part of the paper

Two earlier attempts trained to perfectly reasonable loss curves but had identical validation perplexity at r=1r = 1r=1 and r=32r = 32r=32. The model had found a local minimum in which it ignores the incoming state sss — a non-recurrent model wearing a recurrent architecture. Initialisation and norm placement were what fixed it. If you build one of these, make "perplexity as a function of rrr" your primary training-time diagnostic.

Results and behaviour

  • With few-shot context, easy tasks saturate around r≈8–12r \approx 8\text{--}12r≈8–12; reasoning-heavy tasks keep improving to r=32–64r = 32\text{--}64r=32–64. The saturation point is task-dependent and, notably, correlated with how much reasoning the task needs — which is a free difficulty estimator.
  • Per-token adaptive exit with a KL threshold of 5⋅10−45\cdot 10^{-4}5⋅10−4 works zero-shot — no gate, no extra training. Mean steps to convergence vary sensibly by domain (high-school mathematics 12.7, philosophy 14.6, logical fallacies 15.6, moral scenarios 16.2).
  • Recurrence unlocks per-token adaptive compute, self-speculative decoding, and KV-cache sharing essentially for free — all things that require dedicated engineering in standard models.

4.2 Ouro / LoopLM — looping as a pre-training objective (ByteDance Seed, 2025)

Core idea. Train a shared loop with losses over possible exit depths and an entropy term that discourages a degenerate exit distribution. This makes useful intermediate predictions and depth allocation part of the training objective.

The bet: modest depth (R=4R = 4R=4), but the loop budget is learned, and the whole thing is trained at production scale — 7.7 trillion tokens.

The objective — and why the entropy term exists

L=∑t=1Tmax⁡pϕ(t∣x)L(t)⏟expected task loss−βH(pϕ(⋅∣x))⏟entropy regularizationH(pϕ(⋅∣x))=−∑tpϕ(t∣x)log⁡pϕ(t∣x)\begin{aligned}\mathcal L&=\underbrace{\sum_{t=1}^{T_{\max}}p_\phi(t\mid x)\mathcal L^{(t)}}_{\text{expected task loss}}-\underbrace{\beta H(p_\phi(\cdot\mid x))}_{\text{entropy regularization}}\\ H(p_\phi(\cdot\mid x))&=-\sum_tp_\phi(t\mid x)\log p_\phi(t\mid x)\end{aligned}LH(pϕ​(⋅∣x))​=expected task losst=1∑Tmax​​pϕ​(t∣x)L(t)​​−entropy regularizationβH(pϕ​(⋅∣x))​​=−t∑​pϕ​(t∣x)logpϕ​(t∣x)​

The first term is just "weight each depth's loss by how likely you are to stop there." Left alone it collapses, and the mechanism is worth spelling out because it will bite you in any adaptive-depth design:

The self-reinforcing collapse

As pϕp_\phi pϕ​ shifts mass toward later steps, those steps receive more gradient signal, so their losses drop further, which pulls even more mass toward the end. The equilibrium is pϕp_\phi pϕ​ concentrated entirely on t=Tmax⁡t = T_{\max}t=Tmax​ — adaptive depth that is not adaptive. The entropy bonus is what keeps the distribution spread enough to reflect actual input difficulty. β\beta β is an explicit exploration/exploitation dial.

There is a clean alternative reading: the objective is variational inference with a uniform prior over exit depth, with β\beta β as the KL weight. A separate adaptive gate loss additionally trains the gate against target continuation probabilities derived from measured per-step improvement, penalising "underthinking" (exiting when continuing would have helped) and its converse.

The pipeline

shared warmup → stable training (3T tokens)
      ├── keep 1.4B ──┐
      └── upcycle 2.6B┤   (duplicate the 1.4B layers)
                      ├─► CT annealing (1.4T) → LongCT (20B) → mid-training (300B)
                      └─► Reasoning SFT → Ouro-*-Thinking
total ≈ 7.7T tokens;  released checkpoints use R = 4

Results — read them carefully

Ouro-2.6B-R4 vs. the strongest dense baselines in the paper's own table:

BenchmarkOuro-2.6B (R4)Qwen3-8BGemma3-12BVerdict
MMLU-Pro55.7353.7249.21wins
BBH80.4677.6578.41wins
MATH50090.8562.3083.20wins by a lot
MMLU74.6076.6372.14close
ARC-C66.4066.1072.44loses to 12B
HumanEval78.7084.8046.30loses

The pattern is exactly what §3.3 predicts: wins concentrate on reasoning and math; losses concentrate on knowledge- and commonsense-heavy tasks. A 2.6B looped model is not a free 8B model — it is an 8B-class reasoner with a 2.6B-sized memory.

The mechanism experiment — the most important result in the paper

Recurrence does not add capacity; it adds manipulation

Using controlled experiments in the "physics of LMs" style, the authors measure raw knowledge storage at roughly 2 bits per parameter for looped and non-looped models alike — recurrence changes it not at all. What improves dramatically is knowledge manipulation: fact composition and multi-hop reasoning over facts the model already stores. This is the cleanest available explanation of why looped models behave the way they do on benchmarks.

Two further claims: harmfulness on HEx-PHI decreases as recurrent steps increase (including at extrapolated step counts), and latent iterative updates produce traces better aligned with final outputs than explicit CoT — i.e. greater causal faithfulness, less post-hoc rationalisation. Hold that second claim next to §5, which points the other way.

Derivation: solve the entropy-regularized exit distribution step by step

Fixed per-depth losses. Let ℓt be a measured task loss at depth t, ct its cost, and πt>0 a prior over exits. To expose the optimization, temporarily optimize a free distribution p rather than a neural gate. For β>0 and λ≥0, minimize ∑tpt(ℓt+λct)+β∑tptlog⁡ptπt\sum_tp_t(\ell_t+\lambda c_t)+\beta\sum_tp_t\log\frac{p_t}{\pi_t}∑t​pt​(ℓt​+λct​)+β∑t​pt​logπt​pt​​, subject to Σp=1.

  1. Add a Lagrange multiplier ν(Σp−1).
  2. Set the derivative for each pt to zero: ℓt+λct+β[log(pt/πt)+1]+ν=0.
  3. Exponentiate and absorb the common constant into the normalization Z.
pt∗=πtexp⁡[−(ℓt+λct)/β]ZZ=∑jπjexp⁡[−(ℓj+λcj)/β]Objective⁡(p)=−βlog⁡Z+βDKL(p∥p∗)\begin{aligned}p_t^*&=\frac{\pi_t\exp[-(\ell_t+\lambda c_t)/\beta]}Z\\ Z&=\sum_j\pi_j\exp[-(\ell_j+\lambda c_j)/\beta]\\ \operatorname{Objective}(p)&=-\beta\log Z+\beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|p^*)\end{aligned}pt∗​ZObjective(p)​=Zπt​exp[−(ℓt​+λct​)/β]​=j∑​πj​exp[−(ℓj​+λcj​)/β]=−βlogZ+βDKL​(p∥p∗)​

The last identity proves optimality because KL≥0. For a uniform prior and λ=0, KL(p∥π)=−H(p)+log T, recovering expected loss minus an entropy bonus up to a constant. An entropy bonus spreads exits, but by itself does not price computation: an explicit cost term or nonuniform cost-aware prior is needed for that objective. A geometric prior induces a depth preference through −log πt, approximately linear in t before truncation.

In an actual model, losses and gate probabilities co-evolve, the gate cannot necessarily realize any desired p independently, and training may use additional objectives. The closed form is a diagnostic of the loss, not a claim that Ouro’s learned gates equal p* or that entropy guarantees adaptive behavior. It explains why β controls concentration and why loss improvements must be weighed against computation rather than merely assigned an entropy label.

Exercise — Solve a two-depth exit tradeoff

Two depths have losses (0.6,0.4), costs (1,3), uniform prior, and β=0.1. Find the optimal exit probabilities first with λ=0 and then with λ=0.1. What does the change show?

Show worked solution

With no cost, p₂/p₁=exp((0.6−0.4)/0.1)=e², so p₁=1/(1+e²)≈0.119203 and p₂≈0.880797. With λ=0.1, adjusted losses are 0.6+0.1=0.7 and 0.4+0.3=0.7, so both probabilities are 1/2. Entropy alone does not discourage the more expensive depth; cost changes the relative energy. Expected cost falls from 0.119203+3·0.880797≈2.76159 to 2.
