5Inside the loop: what is the model actually doing?

This is where the field is genuinely unsettled. One camp shows rich, structured latent dynamics; another shows that you cannot read a chain of thought out of them. Both are right, and the reconciliation is the interesting part.

5.1 The latent trajectories are structured

Three behaviours emerge without ever being trained for:

  • Convergence to a fixed point — the DEQ-like default, for tokens that need little work.
  • Orbits — periodic patterns in latent space, appearing on tokens involved in arithmetic and on structural tokens like "makes" or "thinks" that shape the response. Compare to the rotational features found in fixed-depth models trained on arithmetic; here they appear far beyond arithmetic.
  • Sliders — monotone drift in a single direction, a plausible mechanism for counting how many iterations have elapsed, which the model would otherwise have no access to.

Also note: the distance to the fixed point does not always decrease monotonically. The model may take an excursion while processing and come back. "It converged" and "it is done thinking" are not the same statement.

5.2 But you cannot read a chain of thought out of them

Lu et al. probed Huginn on arithmetic with two decoding methods — the logit lens (project a hidden state through the output head directly) and the coda lens (route it through the coda block first, which is the architecturally "correct" decoder). Their findings:

  • Little evidence of interpretable latent CoT. Tracking the rank trajectories of the final and intermediate result tokens shows no smooth convergence toward the answer over iterations.
  • Severe probing inconsistency. Interpretability depends dramatically on both the block index and the decoding method. The same hidden state at R4R_{4}R4​ decodes to {"inc","unity","friendships","igne","impulse"} under the logit lens and to {"6","5","1","7","2"} under the coda lens. At R1R_{1}R1​ the situation reverses. Their conclusion — lens applicability must be assessed per layer — is a warning for anyone probing a recurrent model.
  • Diminishing returns. Increasing recurrence depth yields only marginal accuracy gains on these tasks, well short of models that externalise their reasoning in tokens.

A plausible explanation they offer: R4R_{4}R4​'s output serves a dual role, feeding both the next recurrent cycle (via R1R_{1}R1​) and the coda C1C_{1}C1​, which may force it into a representation unlike the other blocks'.

5.3 How to hold both results at once

The reconciliation

"No readable chain of thought" ≠ "no computation." The logit/coda lens assumes the hidden state is vocabulary-aligned — that intermediate results are stored in a basis the output head can read. A loop has no incentive to maintain that alignment; its intermediate states only need to be readable by the next iteration of itself. The orbit and slider structure in §5.1 is direct evidence of computation in a representation that is deliberately not token-shaped.

This also frames the safety question sharply. The optimistic reading of latent reasoning is that it is more faithful — Ouro measures latent traces as better aligned with final outputs than CoT, which is known to be partly post-hoc rationalisation. The pessimistic reading is that a model reasoning in a non-token basis has no monitorable trace at all. Both follow from the same fact: the trace is real but is not in English.

Open agenda. Better probes (train a decoder per recurrence step rather than reusing the output head), causal interventions (patch a latent state at step ttt and see whether the answer moves), and trajectory-level analysis (a line of work reports that correct and incorrect latent trajectories are strongly separable by entropy, anisotropy, intrinsic dimension and effective rank — enough to build a latent reward model and optimise the trajectory at test time).

Derivation: derive a stopping certificate and show why adjacent KL is weaker

Sufficient contraction assumptions. Suppose, for a fixed input, R is a contraction with constant ρ<1 in a chosen norm and has fixed point s*. Let the one-step residual at state s be r(s)=‖R(s)−s‖. Apply the triangle inequality and contraction:

∥s−s∗∥≤∥s−R(s)∥+∥R(s)−R(s∗)∥≤r(s)+ρ∥s−s∗∥∥s−s∗∥≤r(s)1−ρ\begin{aligned}\|s-s^*\|&\le\|s-R(s)\|+\|R(s)-R(s^*)\|\\ &\le r(s)+\rho\|s-s^*\|\\ \|s-s^*\|&\le\frac{r(s)}{1-\rho}\end{aligned}∥s−s∗∥∥s−s∗∥​≤∥s−R(s)∥+∥R(s)−R(s∗)∥≤r(s)+ρ∥s−s∗∥≤1−ρr(s)​​

If output logits z(s) are L-Lipschitz from this state norm to the infinity norm, then each logit differs from its fixed-point value by at most ε=Lr(s)/(1−ρ). If the current largest logit exceeds the runner-up by more than 2ε, that argmax cannot change at the fixed point: the winner can decrease by ε and the runner-up can increase by ε. This certifies a particular greedy decision under explicit assumptions, not the correctness of the answer.

A small KL between consecutive output distributions provides a different statement. Pinsker bounds the total variation for that one step by √(KL/2), but many small changes can accumulate. Triangle inequality only gives a sum of per-step TV distances, which may grow without a known convergent tail. For example pt(A)=0.4+0.001t changes little each step but crosses 0.5 after 100 steps; its preferred answer changes. Small adjacent KL is an empirical halting signal, not a universal convergence or answer-stability proof. Orbits, drifting states, and state directions invisible to the current readout further weaken that inference.

Exercise — Use a residual bound to certify an argmax

Assume ρ=0.8, a state residual r(s)=0.001, and logit Lipschitz constant L=3. What is the maximum per-logit change to the fixed point? Are current logit gaps 0.02 and 0.04 certified stable?

Show worked solution

The state distance is at most 0.001/(1−0.8)=0.005. Per-logit change is at most 3·0.005=0.015. A sufficient stable-gap condition is strictly greater than 2·0.015=0.03. The 0.02 gap is not certified; it might still remain stable. The 0.04 gap is certified under the stated contraction and Lipschitz assumptions. Neither case proves that the winning token is factually correct.

6The neighbourhood

Problems defining this stage. Adjacent latent-reasoning methods differ in what grows during inference: sequence length, recurrent depth, a puzzle-solving state or the set of active tokens. Comparing those state locations prevents gains from a larger scratchpad or a specialized task from being attributed to depth recurrence alone.

Four adjacent families that are constantly confused with depth-recurrence. The distinctions are sharp once you ask: what is being iterated, and where does the state live?

6.1 Coconut — recurrence over the sequence, not over depth

Core idea. Feed a hidden state back as the embedding of the next latent sequence position instead of decoding and re-embedding a vocabulary token. Computation therefore grows a continuous scratchpad along the sequence rather than repeatedly refining only the same positions.

Coconut is the most important "latent reasoning" method that is not a looped transformer, and keeping the difference straight matters:

CoconutDepth-recurrent / looped
What iteratesThe sequence — one new (latent) position per stepThe depth — same positions, refined
Cost per stepA full-depth forward passOne block application
State between stepsThe growing sequence of continuous thoughts (memory grows)The fixed-size residual stream (memory constant)
Relation to CoTCoT with the vocabulary bottleneck removedA different axis entirely

Coconut keeps CoT's growing scratchpad — so it sits on the token axis of §0.2, just with continuous rather than discrete tokens. Its headline emergent behaviour is that a continuous thought can encode several alternative next steps at once, giving something like a breadth-first search rather than committing to one path; it wins on logical-reasoning tasks needing search (ProsQA) with far fewer tokens. Training uses a multi-stage curriculum with a hyperparameter ccc = latent thoughts per language step; raising ccc from 0 to 1 to 2 monotonically improved results, evidence of genuine chaining.

6.2 HRM and TRM — recursion outside language modelling

Core idea. HRM alternates slow and fast recurrent modules, while TRM repeatedly updates a compact latent and answer state with a smaller shared network. Both rely on iterative refinement and repeated supervision for specialized reasoning tasks.

HRM (Hierarchical Reasoning Model, 27M parameters) uses two recurrent modules at different frequencies — a slow "high-level" planner zHz_HzH​ and a fast "low-level" worker zLz_LzL​ — plus deep supervision and ACT. Trained on ~1000 examples with no pre-training and no CoT supervision, it reached 40.3% on ARC-AGI-1 and ~5% on ARC-AGI-2.

TRM stripped it down: one network instead of two, one latent instead of a hierarchy, no fixed-point theorem, no brain analogy. With 7M parameters and 2 layers it reaches 45% on ARC-AGI-1, 8% on ARC-AGI-2, and 87.4% on Sudoku-Extreme versus HRM's 55.0%. It won the ARC Prize 2025 Paper Award.

Read these numbers carefully

HRM and TRM are trained with supervised learning to predict one specific answer per puzzle type, with heavy augmentation, deep supervision and test-time ensembling. "7M parameters beats DeepSeek R1 on ARC-AGI" is true and also not an apples-to-apples comparison with a general-purpose LM. What the results do establish — robustly — is that recursion plus deep supervision extracts an enormous amount of effective depth from a tiny network. Follow-up work also suggests deep supervision and augmentation, rather than the hierarchy, carry most of HRM's performance.

6.3 Mixture-of-Recursions — making adaptive depth efficient

Core idea. Route tokens through different numbers of shared-block applications and align cache storage with that routing. The architecture couples adaptive depth to recursion-aware attention and KV handling so inactive tokens need not incur every deeper update.

MoR is the answer to "adaptive depth sounds great, but it wrecks batching and KV-caching." Three ideas at once:

  1. Parameter sharing — one recursion block reused, as usual.
  2. Token-level routing — lightweight routers assign each token its own recursion depth; in the expert-choice variant the router keeps the top-kkk tokens at each step and the rest exit. Quadratic attention is then restricted to the tokens still active at that depth.
  3. Recursion-wise KV caching — cache KV only for tokens routed to that depth, shrinking both cache size and memory traffic. A variant reuses the first recursion's KV pairs for all depths, so only the first recursion runs during prefill — a large win for very long prompts.

Across 135M–1.7B parameters MoR forms a new Pareto frontier: lower validation perplexity and better few-shot accuracy at equal training FLOPs, with up to ~2× inference throughput. If you intend to deploy a looped model rather than study one, this is the paper to copy from.

6.4 Two more worth knowing

  • Training-free looped transformers. 2026 preprint Retrofit recurrence onto a frozen checkpoint by looping a contiguous mid-stack block at inference, no fine-tuning. Naively re-applying a block degrades output; the fix comes from viewing a pre-norm block as a forward-Euler step on an ODE, and replacing one large update with several smaller damped sub-steps. Promising if it holds up, because it needs no training run at all.
  • Diffusion language models. Geiping et al. explicitly flag the resemblance: a latent diffusion model also iteratively refines a latent state. They tried diffusion-style variants (adding noise each step, si=R(e,si−1)+ns_{i} = R(e, s_{i-1}) + nsi​=R(e,si−1​)+n) and found the noise injection didn't help, and that conditioning the block on the current step index interacts badly with path independence and kills extrapolation.

7Inference: making loops fast

Problems defining this stage. Serving shifts attention from stored parameter count to repeated weight traffic, depth-indexed KV storage and uneven exit depths. The problem is to reuse the shared computation across active tokens while managing caches and batching without silently changing the model’s predictions.

A looped model has a completely different cost profile from a dense model of the same effective depth — dramatically better in one dimension and dramatically worse in another. This chapter is about exploiting the first and repairing the second.

7.1 The cost model: parameter reuse does not guarantee traffic reuse

k=shared block layers,r=recurrences,B=batchn=context tokens,dh=KV head widthHkv=KV heads,bkv=bytes per cached scalarNstored=Ncore+Nprelude+Ncoda(independent of r)Ftoken=Ffixed+rFcoreMKV≈2rknBHkvdhbkv+Mfixed layersTruncated backprop stores retained depth; gradients are approximate.Each token requires r sequential core applications.\begin{aligned}k&=\text{shared block layers},\quad r=\text{recurrences},\quad B=\text{batch}\\ n&=\text{context tokens},\quad d_h=\text{KV head width}\\ H_{\mathrm{kv}}&=\text{KV heads},\quad b_{\mathrm{kv}}=\text{bytes per cached scalar}\\ N_{\mathrm{stored}}&=N_{\mathrm{core}}+N_{\mathrm{prelude}}+N_{\mathrm{coda}}\quad\text{(independent of }r\text{)}\\ F_{\mathrm{token}}&=F_{\mathrm{fixed}}+rF_{\mathrm{core}}\\ M_{\mathrm{KV}}&\approx2rknBH_{\mathrm{kv}}d_hb_{\mathrm{kv}}+M_{\mathrm{fixed\ layers}}\\ &\text{Truncated backprop stores retained depth; gradients are approximate.}\\ &\text{Each token requires }r\text{ sequential core applications.}\end{aligned}knHkv​Nstored​Ftoken​MKV​​=shared block layers,r=recurrences,B=batch=context tokens,dh​=KV head width=KV heads,bkv​=bytes per cached scalar=Ncore​+Nprelude​+Ncoda​(independent of r)=Ffixed​+rFcore​≈2rknBHkv​dh​bkv​+Mfixed layers​Truncated backprop stores retained depth; gradients are approximate.Each token requires r sequential core applications.​

Weight tying guarantees smaller stored parameter capacity than an untied model of the same effective depth. It does not guarantee that the core weights are fetched from HBM only once. When a core exceeds effective on-chip cache capacity, each invocation reloads its weights; the guide’s measured per-recurrence reload cost δ below is evidence for precisely this regime.

Two different hardware regimes

With N₀ nonrecurrent parameters, Nᵣ shared core parameters, and b bytes per weight, storage is b(N0+Nr)b(N_{0}+N_{r})b(N0​+Nr​). Full per-loop reloading moves b(N0+rNr)b(N_{0}+rN_{r})b(N0​+rNr​) bytes per decode step, while ideal complete on-chip residency moves only b(N0+Nr)b(N_{0}+N_{r})b(N0​+Nr​). The latter requires a capacity and scheduling assumption; it does not follow from sharing a tensor.

For an illustrative Huginn-scale ledger, including the output-head application, N₀≈2B, Nᵣ≈1.5B, r=32 and BF16 give approximately 7 GB stored weights and 100 GFLOPs per sequence. Reloading the 3 GB core each loop moves about 100 GB per step, so batch-one weight-only intensity remains near 1 FLOP/byte. The hypothetical resident-core case gives about 14.3 FLOP/byte, but requires retaining that core at the memory level whose bandwidth is being analyzed.

The defensible deployment advantages are smaller parameter storage, possible fitting on fewer devices, and reuse across tokens that share a core invocation. A reduced saturation batch is conditional on actual traffic reuse; it is not an automatic r-fold gain from recurrence. The stepwise derivation after the measured model below makes the distinction explicit.

The empirical version

The same paper fits a three-term roofline to a recurrent step, which is the model to carry around:

t(Nc,Nb)=δ⏟weight reload+γNb⏟recurrent compute+αNc⏟KV streamingδ: independent of batchNb: batch tokens,Nc: context tokens\begin{aligned}t(N_c,N_b)&=\underbrace{\delta}_{\text{weight reload}}+\underbrace{\gamma N_b}_{\text{recurrent compute}}+\underbrace{\alpha N_c}_{\text{KV streaming}}\\ \delta&:\ \text{independent of batch}\\ N_b&:\ \text{batch tokens},\quad N_c:\ \text{context tokens}\end{aligned}t(Nc​,Nb​)δNb​​=weight reloadδ​​+recurrent computeγNb​​​+KV streamingαNc​​​: independent of batch: batch tokens,Nc​: context tokens​
…and the KV cache takes the gift back

A per-loop KV cache grows linearly with r relative to a one-pass model using the same k shared layers. Relative to an untied model of equal effective depth kr and equal attention dimensions, both have comparable numbers of layer-specific KV entries. The loop’s smaller parameter storage therefore need not imply a smaller cache. At long context, this traffic can dominate core execution, motivating the approximations and trained cache-sharing architectures in §7.2.

Derivation: derive weight capacity versus weight traffic for a shared recurrent core

Do not equate a stored tensor with one memory read. Let N₀ be nonrecurrent parameters used once per token, Nr shared core parameters, r loop iterations, B active sequences, and b bytes per weight. Let q be the number of times the core weights cross HBM during one decode step. A full reload at every loop gives q=r; persistent on-chip residency across all loops gives q=1.

Mweights=b(N0+Nr)(independent of r)Fmatmul≈2B(N0+rNr)Bweights/step=b(N0+qNr),1≤q≤rIweights=2B(N0+rNr)b(N0+qNr)\begin{aligned}M_{\mathrm{weights}}&=b(N_0+N_r)\quad\text{(independent of }r\text{)}\\ F_{\mathrm{matmul}}&\approx2B(N_0+rN_r)\\ B_{\mathrm{weights/step}}&=b(N_0+qN_r),\quad1\le q\le r\\ I_{\mathrm{weights}}&=\frac{2B(N_0+rN_r)}{b(N_0+qN_r)}\end{aligned}Mweights​Fmatmul​Bweights/step​Iweights​​=b(N0​+Nr​)(independent of r)≈2B(N0​+rNr​)=b(N0​+qNr​),1≤q≤r=b(N0​+qNr​)2B(N0​+rNr​)​​
  1. Under full reload, q=r and intensity simplifies to 2B/b, the same weight-only intensity as an untied stack of equal effective depth.
  2. Under full residency, q=1 and intensity improves by the factor (N₀+rNr)/(N₀+Nr).
  3. The residency case requires sufficient effective on-chip capacity and a schedule that preserves the weights while activations, attention state, and other operations run. Weight tying alone supplies neither.

Illustrative Huginn-scale ledger: N₀≈2B including the nonrecurrent layers and a fully applied shared output head, Nr≈1.5B, r=32, BF16 b=2. Stored weights are about 7 GB; work is about 100 GFLOPs per sequence. Full reload moves approximately 4+32·3=100 GB of weights per step, giving about 1 FLOP/byte at batch one. Ideal full residency would move 7 GB and give approximately 14.29 FLOP/byte, but a 3 GB core does not fit in the ordinary on-chip cache of a single current GPU. The latter is a conditional hardware scenario, not the default Huginn cost.

With weight traffic M and per-sequence work f, the weight-only saturation batch is MF/(fBw). Reloading approximately cancels the r increase in work against the r increase in traffic; it does not automatically divide the saturation batch by r. Smaller stored capacity can still make the model fit on fewer devices or permit more replicas. Continuous depth batching can improve reuse across different tokens in the same core invocation; that is distinct from retaining a whole core across successive loops.

Exercise — Calculate both residency regimes

A model has N₀=0.5B nonrecurrent parameters, Nr=1B core parameters, r=8, BF16 weights, and B=1. Compute stored bytes, approximate FLOPs, HBM weight traffic, and intensity for q=8 and q=1. Which quantity is guaranteed to shrink through weight tying?

Show worked solution

Stored weights are 2(0.5+1)=3 GB. Work is 2(0.5+8)=17 GFLOPs. With q=8, traffic is 2(0.5+8)=17 GB and intensity 1 FLOP/byte. With q=1, traffic is 3 GB and intensity 17/3≈5.667 FLOP/byte. The parameter/storage capacity is reduced relative to eight distinct core copies. The low-traffic q=1 case additionally needs residency or equivalent weight reuse at the relevant memory boundary; it does not follow from equal tensor addresses alone.

7.2 The KV cache problem, and seven answers

Core idea. Looped Latent Attention compresses a token’s trajectory of KV vectors across recurrent depth into a low-rank latent and reconstructs the depth-specific vectors on demand. MELT instead evolves a shared cache through a learned state update; both change the cache representation and require their stated training or distillation procedures.

Every approach below is a different way of refusing to store one vector per loop. They compose with each other and with the ordinary tricks, and they sit at very different points on the training-cost axis.

ApproachMechanismCost / benefit
Cross-loop reuse
zero-shot		 Reuse the first loop's KV entry for all later loops, or share entries periodically across recurrent steps. May require no additional training. Shared projections make reuse convenient, but hidden states change across loops, so substituting cache entries is generally approximate. Geiping et al. evaluate such reuse on Huginn. Quality and runtime must be measured for the selected reuse policy; implementation still requires explicit cache management.
Recursive KV sharing
(MoR)		 The same idea trained in: cache only at the first recursion, reuse it at every subsequent depth. Also lets you skip the KV projection — and part of prefill — at shared depths, which is a large win for long prompts. The catch the MoR authors flag: a recursive model has far fewer free parameters available to absorb the tying than a vanilla model does, so the quality cost is bigger than the same trick applied to a dense stack.
Recursion-wise caching
(MoR, T-LoopFormer)		 Keep a separate cache per loop, but write and attend to entries only for tokens still active at that depth. Matches memory to actual work: as tokens exit in deeper recursions, the cache naturally shrinks. Requires token-level routing, and makes the cache ragged — see §7.3.
Last-exited cache
(CDB)		 When a token exits at depth rt<rmax⁡r_t < r_{\max}rt​<rmax​, copy its final state into the slots for the steps it skipped. Copy-on-exit. Cheap, and it solves the ragged-cache problem — a later, deeper token always finds something to attend to — without recomputation. The pragmatic default.
Cross-loop latent compression
(LLA) 2026		 For each (layer, head, token), treat the TTT per-loop K/V vectors as a trajectory and store a single low-rank latent c=(x−μ)Wdownc = (x - \mu )W_{\mathrm{down}}c=(x−μ)Wdown​; reconstruct x^t=cWup,t⊤+μt\widehat x_t=cW_{\mathrm{up},t}^\top+\mu_txt​=cWup,t⊤​+μt​ per loop, before RoPE. Retrofits onto a frozen model by distillation. Justified by the empirical finding that the cross-loop K/V trajectory is low-rank and stabilises with depth — the same structural fact §5.1 sees as convergence. Adds a small matmul on the decode path.
Constant-memory state
(MELT) 2026		 Don't grow the cache at all. Keep one KV entry per layer per token and evolve it across loops through a learned gate. O(1)O(1)O(1) in depth — recovers a non-looped model's footprint exactly. Requires two-phase distillation from a LoopLM teacher, and training is sequential across tokens, which limits parallelism.
Parallel Loop Transformer Global KV taken from the first loop, supplemented by local sliding-window attention over the current loop's representations. Paired with cross-loop parallelism so different tokens occupy different loops in one pass. Reported +5.0 average benchmark points over a vanilla baseline at +2% latency and +1.4% KV memory for two loops — the strongest published cost/benefit at small rrr.
The ordinary tricks GQA / MQA, MLA, cross-layer attention, KV quantization. All compose with the above and are orthogonal to the loop axis. Apply them first — they are cheaper and better understood.
zt=σ(xtWz+ht−1Uz+bz)(learned gate)ht=zt⊙ht−1+(1−zt)⊙xtkt=htWK,vt=htWV(derived, not appended)MLoopLM=O(LT)⟶MMELT=O(L)Latent state size is independent of depth.\begin{aligned}z_t&=\sigma(x_tW_z+h_{t-1}U_z+b_z)\quad\text{(learned gate)}\\ h_t&=z_t\odot h_{t-1}+(1-z_t)\odot x_t\\ k_t&=h_tW_K,\quad v_t=h_tW_V\quad\text{(derived, not appended)}\\ M_{\mathrm{LoopLM}}&=O(LT)\quad\longrightarrow\quad M_{\mathrm{MELT}}=O(L)\\ &\text{Latent state size is independent of depth.}\end{aligned}zt​ht​kt​MLoopLM​​=σ(xt​Wz​+ht−1​Uz​+bz​)(learned gate)=zt​⊙ht−1​+(1−zt​)⊙xt​=ht​WK​,vt​=ht​WV​(derived, not appended)=O(LT)⟶MMELT​=O(L)Latent state size is independent of depth.​
The shape of every answer here

All seven replace "store a vector per loop" with "store one thing and reconstruct or update it." That is precisely the move MLA makes along the head axis and CLA makes along the layer axis — applied instead to the recurrence axis. If you already understand why MLA works, you already understand this family; the only new question is whether the cross-loop trajectory is compressible, and the empirical answer (LLA's low-rank finding, Huginn's convergence behaviour) is that it is.

Derivation: bound the error from substituting a shallower loop cache

Same projections, different states. At one token, two recurrence depths have hidden states h and h̃. With shared linear projections k=AKh and v=AVh, equality of the matrices only ensures compatible dimensions and coordinates. The cache vectors differ unless the projections annihilate the hidden-state difference.

Δk=AK(h~−h),Δv=AV(h~−h)∥Δk∥≤∥AK∥∥Δh∥,∥Δv∥≤∥AV∥∥Δh∥∣Δscore∣=∣q⊤Δk∣d≤∥q∥∥AK∥∥Δh∥d\begin{aligned}\Delta k&=A_K(\widetilde h-h),\quad\Delta v=A_V(\widetilde h-h)\\ \|\Delta k\|&\le\|A_K\|\|\Delta h\|,\quad\|\Delta v\|\le\|A_V\|\|\Delta h\|\\ |\Delta\mathrm{score}|&=\frac{|q^\top\Delta k|}{\sqrt d}\\ &\le\frac{\|q\|\|A_K\|\|\Delta h\|}{\sqrt d}\end{aligned}Δk∥Δk∥∣Δscore∣​=AK​(h−h),Δv=AV​(h−h)≤∥AK​∥∥Δh∥,∥Δv∥≤∥AV​∥∥Δh∥=d​∣q⊤Δk∣​≤d​∥q∥∥AK​∥∥Δh∥​​

Assume each cached score changes by at most δ and each value by at most εv, with original value norms ≤V. The softmax Jacobian applied to a perturbation u has coordinates pi(ui−Σpjuj), whose L1 norm is at most 2‖u‖∞. Integrating along the straight line between score vectors yields ‖p̃−p‖₁≤min(2,2δ). Splitting the output change into changed probabilities and changed values gives:

∥∑jp~jv~j−∑jpjvj∥≤∥∑j(p~j−pj)vj∥+∥∑jp~j(v~j−vj)∥≤Vmin⁡(2,2δ)+εv\begin{aligned}\left\|\sum_j\widetilde p_j\widetilde v_j-\sum_jp_jv_j\right\|&\le\left\|\sum_j(\widetilde p_j-p_j)v_j\right\|\\ &\quad+\left\|\sum_j\widetilde p_j(\widetilde v_j-v_j)\right\|\\ &\le V\min(2,2\delta)+\varepsilon_v\end{aligned}​j∑​p​j​vj​−j∑​pj​vj​​​≤​j∑​(p​j​−pj​)vj​​+​j∑​p​j​(vj​−vj​)​≤Vmin(2,2δ)+εv​​

This bound explains when cross-loop reuse may be accurate: hidden states or their projected keys/values must already be close enough in relevant directions. Tied weights do not establish that premise. Different RoPE positions, changing queries, normalization, and later layers require additional terms. Cache substitution is an approximation to the original per-depth model unless a specific architecture defines the shared cache as its native computation.

For cross-loop low-rank compression, stack loop-specific vectors into a training data matrix X and approximate it with rank m. The best unconstrained rank-m reconstruction in Frobenius norm has squared error Σj>mσj², the discarded singular values. That is a reconstruction optimum on X, not a task-loss or out-of-distribution guarantee. LLA-style distillation asks whether real loop trajectories are compressible enough to make that storage/compute trade worthwhile.

Exercise — Tied projections do not imply identical KV

Let AK=I₂, h=(1,0), h̃=(0,1), q=(1,0), and head width d=2. Compute both attention scores. If the same projection matrices are used at both depths, is replacing the first key by the second exact?

Show worked solution

The keys are k=(1,0) and k̃=(0,1). Scores are qᵀk/√2=1/√2≈0.707107 and qᵀk̃/√2=0. Their difference is nonzero even though AK is identical. Therefore the replacement is not exact in general. With multiple cached positions, it changes relative logits and usually the attention distribution; shape compatibility is insufficient.

7.3 Adaptive depth and the batching problem

Core idea. Continuous depth batching groups tokens that currently need the same shared computation even if they are at different logical depths. Its cache policy supplies representations for previously exited tokens, addressing the mismatch between adaptive exits and attention over the full prefix.

Per-token adaptive compute is the headline feature of every architecture in §4. It is also the thing that breaks the serving stack, because standard continuous batching treats one forward pass as one scheduling unit — so every token in a batch must run the same number of loops. The moment tokens exit at different depths the batch is ragged, and the scheduler has no vocabulary for it.

Why this works, and only here

Because the same function is applied at every depth. In a standard transformer, "stage 3" and "stage 1" are different weight matrices and cannot share a matmul. In a looped model they are the same matrices, so a token on its first pass through the core and a token on its fourth can be batched together. Depth becomes a batching dimension alongside the sequence dimension. An oracle-exit analysis puts the ceiling at 2–3× throughput, beating continuous sequence-wise batching on a vanilla model.

The engineering that makes it work, and which you would have to reinvent otherwise:

  • Refill vs. no-refill. In no-refill mode the stages run in fixed order and exited tokens simply leave. In refill mode a freed slot is immediately filled by another token — possible only because the core reuses the same weights at every loop step, so a token on its first pass and one on its fourth share the layers.
  • A priority rule. The coda gets highest priority because it finishes requests and therefore frees KV, which lets more prompts be admitted. But running a multi-layer coda every time a single token exits is wasteful, so there is a minimum coda batch size — at the cost of tokens taking longer to return to the recurrent queue.
  • Lookahead gating and asynchronous batch preparation, so the CPU assembles batch N+1N+1N+1 from step NNN's exit decisions while the GPU is still working. This hides essentially all per-step scheduling overhead — necessary, because the scheduler now runs once per loop, not once per token.

Measured on Ouro-1.4B and Huginn-3.5B, this tracks the theoretical speed-up bound closely. It is the first end-to-end serving method for depth-adaptive looped models, and it is very recent.

The counterintuitive result, and the best thing in this chapter

Below B∗B^*B∗, early exit saves FLOPs but not wall-clock time. In the memory-bound regime a recurrent step costs δ\delta δ — the weight reload — regardless of how many tokens are in the batch. So when tokens exit and the batch shrinks, the step still takes δ\delta δ and you have saved nothing measurable. Refill mode recovers the loss by spending the otherwise-idle compute on new tokens. Above B∗B^*B∗, wall-clock time tracks total work and early exits pay off directly, with or without refill.

This is the cleanest example anywhere in this series of why "fewer FLOPs" and "less time" are different claims — and it means the value of adaptive depth depends on which side of the roofline knee you are serving.

How much can early exit possibly save?

S≤F0+rmax⁡FrF0+dˉFr≤rmax⁡dˉ≤rmax⁡rmin⁡F0=prelude and coda FLOPsFr=one recurrent step FLOPs,dˉ=mean exit depth\begin{aligned}S&\le\frac{F_0+r_{\max}F_r}{F_0+\bar dF_r}\le\frac{r_{\max}}{\bar d}\le\frac{r_{\max}}{r_{\min}}\\ F_0&=\text{prelude and coda FLOPs}\\ F_r&=\text{one recurrent step FLOPs},\quad\bar d=\text{mean exit depth}\end{aligned}SF0​Fr​​≤F0​+dˉFr​F0​+rmax​Fr​​≤dˉrmax​​≤rmin​rmax​​=prelude and coda FLOPs=one recurrent step FLOPs,dˉ=mean exit depth​
  • Ouro: the prelude and coda are only the token embedding and the LM head, so F0≪FrF_{0} \ll F_rF0​≪Fr​ and the bound is close to rmax⁡dˉ\frac{r_{\max}}{\bar d}dˉrmax​​. With rmax⁡=4r_{\max} = 4rmax​=4, one step fewer saves about 25% of per-token FLOPs.
  • Huginn: the 2–4–2 split means prelude and coda together cost about as much as the recurrent core (F0≈1.2FrF_{0} \approx 1.2 F_rF0​≈1.2Fr​), so the bound falls well below rmax⁡dˉ\frac{r_{\max}}{\bar d}dˉrmax​​. With rmax⁡=16r_{\max} = 16rmax​=16, one step fewer saves only about 6%.
Design implication — and it points back to §1.3

Nonrecurrent work limits the saving from early exit. Its importance is set by its FLOP cost relative to the repeated core, not by parameter count alone. For example, F₀=4 GFLOPs, Fᵣ=3 GFLOPs, rₘₐₓ=32 and mean depth 12 give a work ratio (4+96)/(4+36)=2.5×, versus the zero-overhead ceiling 32/12≈2.67×. A large stored prelude/coda can therefore have a modest compute share when the core repeats many times; quantify the ratio before drawing an architectural conclusion.

Derivation: derive the early-exit compute ceiling and the no-refill latency counterexample

Compute-only ceiling. Fixed prelude/coda work per token is F₀≥0, one recurrent step costs Fr>0, the fixed baseline uses rmax, and adaptive exits have mean depth d̄. Ideal compute work per token changes from F₀+rmaxFr to F₀+d̄Fr. If runtime were proportional to useful work with no scheduling overhead:

Swork=F0+rmax⁡FrF0+dˉFr≤rmax⁡dˉdˉ(F0+rmax⁡Fr)≤rmax⁡(F0+dˉFr)⟺dˉF0≤rmax⁡F0(dˉ≤rmax⁡)dˉ≥rmin⁡  ⟹  Swork≤rmax⁡rmin⁡\begin{aligned}S_{\mathrm{work}}&=\frac{F_0+r_{\max}F_r}{F_0+\bar dF_r}\le\frac{r_{\max}}{\bar d}\\ \bar d(F_0+r_{\max}F_r)&\le r_{\max}(F_0+\bar dF_r)\\ \Longleftrightarrow\quad\bar dF_0&\le r_{\max}F_0\quad(\bar d\le r_{\max})\\ \bar d\ge r_{\min}&\implies S_{\mathrm{work}}\le\frac{r_{\max}}{r_{\min}}\end{aligned}Swork​dˉ(F0​+rmax​Fr​)⟺dˉF0​dˉ≥rmin​​=F0​+dˉFr​F0​+rmax​Fr​​≤dˉrmax​​≤rmax​(F0​+dˉFr​)≤rmax​F0​(dˉ≤rmax​)⟹Swork​≤rmin​rmax​​​

This is not a universal wall-clock upper bound across different kernels or hardware utilization; it is the saving available from work reduction alone under a fixed cost-per-FLOP model. In a memory-bound no-refill batch, suppose a core invocation costs nearly δ as long as at least one token remains. A batch with exits (1,1,1,8) performs only 11 useful token-iterations instead of 32, but still launches eight rounds. If the longest token exits at the baseline depth, its total round time stays about 8δ. Earlier requests can finish sooner if coda scheduling permits, even though batch completion time does not improve.

Refill makes freed slots useful by admitting other tokens into later core invocations. Since the core matrices are shared, tokens at different recurrence depths can participate in one GEMM, provided each retains the right state, position metadata, depth conditioning, and cache policy. The next autoregressive token still depends on completing the current token’s output decision. Sustained gains need enough independent queued work; the same argument cannot create concurrency for a single dependent token stream.

7.4 Self-speculative decoding: reuse the depth-indexed model family

Core idea. Use a shallow recurrent state to propose a next token while deeper states continue toward the target computation. Shared weights allow speculative tokens at different depths to be co-scheduled, with rejection pruning the dependent speculative work.

A looped model provides shallow and deeper executions with shared weights. A shallow execution can draft for a deeper target without a separate full draft checkpoint, but draft states, speculative KV branches, verification, and correction still cost memory and time. Output-distribution preservation follows from the verifier’s sampling law and cache handling, not from parameter sharing alone. A fixed-depth transformer can also self-draft with suitable early exits or layer skipping.

Vanilla looped decode, R = 4 — strictly serial:

  tok t    [1][2][3][4]
  tok t+1              [1][2][3][4]
  tok t+2                           [1][2][3][4]

LoopSpec, first proposal at depth d₁ = 1 — pipelined:

  tok t    [1][2][3][4]
                  └── verify the draft against the final state
  tok t+1     [1][2][3][4]
            ↑ starts from tok t's depth-1 draft, in the same batch
              (same weights at every depth, so they co-schedule)

  accept → those recurrent steps were real work; t+1 is nearly done
  reject → prune the speculative branch and restart  (a pipeline stall)

The refinements that make it work in practice:

  • A residual second proposal. A deeper state d2d_{2}d2​ produces an alternative continuation before verification, so a first-proposal rejection falls back to that branch instead of flushing the pipeline. A gating mechanism only spawns the fallback when the deeper state actually disagrees with the first draft, limiting the overhead.
  • A closed-form choice of depths. The restart probability is proven to depend only on d2d_{2}d2​, not d1d_{1}d1​; combined with the empirically observed power-law decay of the intermediate-to-target total-variation distance, this gives optimal proposal depths in closed form that match the measured optima.
  • Results: up to 6.83× lossless speedup across seven checkpoints from two looped families, training-free, implemented in SGLang with branch-wise KV management and CUDA graphs — up to 1.7× over a training-based baseline.
Measure agreement across depths

Shared weights may make shallow and deep predictions similar, but can also produce different intermediate outputs, oscillations, or late refinements. For one exact stochastic proposal, acceptance is 1−TV⁡(ptarget,pdraft)1-\operatorname{TV}(p_{\mathrm{target}},p_{\mathrm{draft}})1−TV(ptarget​,pdraft​); weight tying does not upper-bound that TV distance. Measure agreement by depth, task, and sampling configuration. Under a constant conditional acceptance approximation, α=0.9 and eight proposals yield (1−0.9⁹)/(1−0.9)≈6.13 emitted tokens including the bonus or correction token.

Two caveats

It spends additional draft and verification resources. Net benefit depends on accepted progress per unit of incremental cost, including KV traffic and scheduling. A compute-saturated batch can lose throughput, while a KV-bound batch may still benefit. Recurrence does not automatically move the model into the compute-bound regime at a smaller batch; that depends on actual weight traffic (§7.1).

It fights with depth batching. Both techniques want to decide what occupies the batch, and they want different things: CDB wants freed slots filled with new tokens, speculation wants them filled with speculative continuations. The CDB authors list combining the two as future work — this is an open systems problem, not a solved one.

7.5 What this asks of silicon

If you are specifying an accelerator and looped models are in your target workload, the requirements are genuinely different from dense serving — in places inverted.

  1. The weight working set is kkk layers, not LLL. This is the headline and it is easy to miss. A looped model needs only one block's weights resident to run to any depth. Huginn's core is 1.5B parameters — 750 MB at INT4, still off-chip — but a 100M-parameter core at 4 bits is 50 MB, which is squarely in SRAM-only territory. Looped models are the architecture most amenable to keeping all weights on-chip, because depth costs time rather than capacity. If you are building an SRAM-centric inference part, this is your natural workload, and the synergy is much stronger than for dense models.
  2. Design for small batch. BsatB_{\mathrm{sat}}Bsat​ falls by roughly rrr (§7.1): ~21 instead of ~300 for Huginn on an H100. A part targeting looped models can be compute-bound at batch 8 where a dense part needs 300. That shifts the whole design point — relatively less HBM bandwidth, relatively more arithmetic, shallower queues, and far better single-user latency.
  3. Budget against the KV cache, not the weights. The dense intuition is inverted. Weight traffic is amortised rrr×; KV traffic is multiplied rrr×. Size bandwidth and capacity against the cache, and assume at least one of the §7.2 techniques is in play.
  4. Ragged, depth-indexed batches are the native workload. The scheduler runs inside the forward pass, re-forming the active token set between block applications. Cheap gather/scatter over a variable active set — and the ability to change batch composition without a host round-trip — is worth real area. The CDB paper spends most of its engineering effort hiding exactly this cost in software.
  5. A cheap exit-decision path. A KL between consecutive output distributions, or a small gate head, evaluated every loop for every token. Tiny arithmetic, but it sits on the critical path and must not become a round trip to HBM.
  6. Persistent state residency across iterations. The latent state sss (and, for MELT-style designs, the gated KV state) is read and written every loop. If it spills to HBM you have rebuilt the problem you were avoiding.
  7. Do not specialise for one rrr. Test-time depth is the product feature; the loop count is a user-visible quality/latency dial and will vary per request, per token, and across model generations.

7.6 If you want to try this on an existing model

In increasing order of cost:

  1. Looping-inspired regularisation (Saunshi et al.). Keep your architecture; add a term pulling each kkk-layer block's weights toward their shared mean. At k=4,λreg=10k = 4, \lambda _{\mathrm{reg}} = 10k=4,λreg​=10 they saw neutral perplexity with large reasoning gains. Cheapest possible experiment.
  2. Training-free looping of a mid-stack block, with damped sub-steps. 2026 preprint No training.
  3. Middle looping from scratch. Keep the first and last layers distinct, loop the middle. Better perplexity and more uniform gains than looping everything — but see the §7.3 warning about what a fat prelude and coda cost you at serving time.
  4. Upcycling. Duplicate an existing model's layers to form a deeper shared block and continue pre-training — how Ouro-2.6B was built from Ouro-1.4B.
  5. Full recurrent pre-training with sampled rrr and truncated BPTT. The Huginn recipe. Expensive, and the failure modes in §4.1 are real.
Starting hyperparameters, if you have nothing else

Modelling: block size k=4k = 4k=4; input injection on; random s0s_{0}s0​; sandwich norm; sample rrr from log-normal Poisson with rˉ\bar rrˉ = your target test-time depth and σ=12\sigma = \frac12σ=21​; truncate backprop at ktrunc=8k_{\mathrm{trunc}} = 8ktrunc​=8; same rrr across data-parallel workers; monitor validation perplexity at r∈{1,4,rˉ,2rˉ}r\in\{1,4,\bar r,2\bar r\}r∈{1,4,rˉ,2rˉ} from step one.

Serving: start with cross-loop KV reuse (free, zero-shot) plus a last-exited cache; add self-speculative decoding before anything else, since it is training-free and the acceptance rate is structurally high; only then invest in depth batching, and only if you are serving above B∗B^*B∗ or can use refill.

8Open problems

Ranked by how much I'd expect an answer to change the field.

  1. Is there latent reasoning, and how would we know? §5 shows rich latent dynamics and unreadable probes simultaneously. We need probing methods that don't assume vocabulary alignment, plus causal interventions. Until then, claims about "latent chain of thought" are under-determined in both directions.
  2. Depth plus memory. The memory-budget separation and the UT-needs-memory result both say a compressed loop is a small-space reasoner. The obvious move — give the loop a scratchpad (memory tokens, a writable buffer, or interleaved token emission) — is where I would bet the next real capability jump comes from.
  3. Halting that actually works. KL thresholds are unprincipled; learned gates collapse without entropy bonuses; ACT is famously fiddly. Nobody has a halting criterion that is stable, calibrated, and cheap.
  4. The inductive bias is unexplained. Why does weight tying push a model toward reasoning at the cost of perplexity? Saunshi et al. state explicitly that this is open. An answer would tell us when to loop and when not to.
  5. Training recipes. Truncated BPTT is a hack; the 1-step gradient is worse than people assumed (TRM's ablation); full BPTT doesn't scale. There is no standard, and the stability failures are silent — a model that has learned to ignore its recurrence looks perfectly healthy on a loss curve.
  6. The KV cache is now the binding constraint. Weight traffic is amortised rrr× but KV traffic is multiplied by it (§7.1), so depth-recurrent models are cheap in the dimension everyone optimises and expensive in the one that actually limits long-context serving. Seven distinct answers exist (§7.2) and none is clearly dominant: the zero-shot ones are free but lossy, the good ones (MELT, LLA) need distillation, and nobody has measured them against each other on a common benchmark.
  7. Serving stacks are only just catching up. Dynamic depth violates the "one forward pass = one scheduling unit" assumption of every production engine. Continuous depth batching (§7.3) is the first end-to-end answer and is very recent; combining it with speculative decoding, tensor parallelism and chunked prefill is explicitly listed as future work by its own authors. Meanwhile the released Ouro implementation still computes all configured passes before selecting an output — the adaptive depth is trained but not yet exploited.
  8. The prelude/coda tension. Quality wants substantial non-recurrent layers at the ends (§1.3, §4.1); adaptive-depth serving wants them as thin as possible, because every FLOP outside the loop is paid regardless of exit depth (§7.3). Nobody has characterised the optimum, and the two published systems sit at opposite extremes.
  9. Does it compose with RL? Every frontier reasoning model is now post-trained with RL on CoT traces. Nobody has convincingly shown what RL does to a looped model, where there are no token-level traces to assign credit to.

In the order I'd read them, with the reason.

  17. servingBae et al. — Relaxed Recursive Transformers: Effective Parameter Sharing with Layer-wise LoRA (2024). arXiv:2410.20672. §2.4 introduces continuous depth-wise batching — the observation that weight tying creates a batching dimension that does not exist in a dense model.   18. servingDepth-adaptive Inference of Looped Language Models via Continuous Depth Batching (2026). arXiv:2608.09444. The end-to-end system: four-queue scheduler, refill mode, depth-aware KV layouts, and a three-term roofline for the recurrent step. The most useful single paper for anyone who has to run one of these.
  19. servingLoopSpec: Pipelined Self-Speculative Decoding for Looped Transformers (2026). arXiv:2609.17184. Training-free, up to 6.83× lossless; the closed-form proposal-depth derivation is the elegant part.
  20. servingKV-cache work: Memory-Efficient Looped Transformer (MELT), arXiv:2605.07721, for constant-memory depth via a gated latent state; Looped Latent Attention, arXiv:2607.15456, for cross-loop low-rank compression that retrofits onto a frozen model; Parallel Loop Transformer, arXiv:2510.24824, for global-first-loop KV plus a local window; and T-LoopFormer, arXiv:2609.15160, for token-level elastic depth with recursion-wise caching.
  21. The companion LLM Inference Systems guide in this series covers the dense-serving background these papers assume — roofline, BsatB_{\mathrm{sat}}Bsat​, PagedAttention, continuous batching, speculative decoding and quantization.

A continuously updated list lives at huskydoge/Awesome-Loop-Models.

ADerivations

A.1 Implicit differentiation for fixed-point (DEQ) models

Suppose the loop converges to a fixed point z∗z^*z∗ satisfying z∗=fθ(z∗,x)z^* = f_\theta (z^*, x)z∗=fθ​(z∗,x). We want ∂L∂θ\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\theta}∂θ∂L​ without storing the unrolled graph. Differentiate the fixed-point equation with respect to θ\theta θ:

∂z∗∂θ=∂f∂z∣z∗∂z∗∂θ+∂f∂θ∣z∗(I−Jf(z∗))∂z∗∂θ=∂f∂θ∂z∗∂θ=(I−Jf(z∗))−1∂f∂θ,Jf=∂f∂z∂L∂θ=∂L∂z∗(I−Jf(z∗))−1∂f∂θ\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial z^*}{\partial\theta}&=\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\right|_{z^*}\frac{\partial z^*}{\partial\theta}+\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta}\right|_{z^*}\\ (I-J_f(z^*))\frac{\partial z^*}{\partial\theta}&=\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta}\\ \frac{\partial z^*}{\partial\theta}&=(I-J_f(z^*))^{-1}\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta},\quad J_f=\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\\ \frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\theta}&=\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial z^*}(I-J_f(z^*))^{-1}\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta}\end{aligned}∂θ∂z∗​(I−Jf​(z∗))∂θ∂z∗​∂θ∂z∗​∂θ∂L​​=∂z∂f​​z∗​∂θ∂z∗​+∂θ∂f​​z∗​=∂θ∂f​=(I−Jf​(z∗))−1∂θ∂f​,Jf​=∂z∂f​=∂z∗∂L​(I−Jf​(z∗))−1∂θ∂f​​

The inverse is never formed. Instead one solves the linear system (I−Jf⊤)u=(∂L∂z∗)⊤(I-J_f^\top)u=\left(\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial z^*}\right)^\top(I−Jf⊤​)u=(∂z∗∂L​)⊤ with a matrix-free iterative solver, using vector–Jacobian products from autograd. Memory is O(1)O(1)O(1) in the number of iterations, because only z∗z^*z∗ is needed.

Why this matters for looped LMs. The 1-step gradient used by HRM is the crude approximation (I−Jf)−1≈I(I-J_f)^{-1}\approx I(I−Jf​)−1≈I, i.e. just backprop through the last application. It is valid only if JfJ_fJf​ is small — if the recursion is strongly contractive. TRM's ablation (§6.2) shows that when that assumption fails, the cost is enormous: 56.5% vs 87.4% on Sudoku-Extreme. Truncated BPTT through kkk steps is the intermediate option: it keeps the first kkk terms of the Neumann series (I−J)−1=I+J+J2+…(I - J)^{-1} = I + J + J^{2} + \ldots (I−J)−1=I+J+J2+….

A.2 Adaptive Computation Time

At each step ttt a unit emits a halting score ht=σ(W⋅st+b)∈(0,1)h_{t} = \sigma (W\cdot s_{t} + b) \in (0,1)ht​=σ(W⋅st​+b)∈(0,1). Accumulate until the total crosses 1−ε1 - \varepsilon 1−ε:

N=min⁡ ⁣{m:∑t=1mht≥1−ε}pt=ht(t<N)pN=R=1−∑t<Nht(remainder)sˉ=∑t=1NptstLtotal=Ltask(sˉ)+τ(N+R)⏟ponder cost\begin{aligned}N&=\min\!\left\{m:\sum_{t=1}^mh_t\ge1-\varepsilon\right\}\\ p_t&=h_t\quad(t<N)\\ p_N&=R=1-\sum_{t<N}h_t\quad\text{(remainder)}\\ \bar s&=\sum_{t=1}^Np_ts_t\\ \mathcal L_{\mathrm{total}}&=\mathcal L_{\mathrm{task}}(\bar s)+\underbrace{\tau(N+R)}_{\text{ponder cost}}\end{aligned}Npt​pN​sˉLtotal​​=min{m:t=1∑m​ht​≥1−ε}=ht​(t<N)=R=1−t<N∑​ht​(remainder)=t=1∑N​pt​st​=Ltask​(sˉ)+ponder costτ(N+R)​​​

The ponder cost τ\tau τ trades accuracy against average depth. The classic complaint is that gradients through NNN are ill-behaved and τ\tau τ is very sensitive. PonderNet replaces this with an explicit distribution over halting steps — pn=λn∏j<n(1−λj)p_n=\lambda_n\prod_{j<n}(1-\lambda_j)pn​=λn​∏j<n​(1−λj​), a Markov halting process — trained with a KL regulariser toward a geometric prior, which gives better-behaved gradients.

A.3 The entropy-regularised exit objective, as variational inference

Ouro's objective (§4.2) is

L=∑tpϕ(t∣x)L(t)−βH(pϕ(⋅∣x))\begin{aligned}\mathcal L&=\sum_tp_\phi(t\mid x)\mathcal L^{(t)}-\beta H(p_\phi(\cdot\mid x))\end{aligned}L​=t∑​pϕ​(t∣x)L(t)−βH(pϕ​(⋅∣x))​

Write the entropy out and add the constant log⁡Tmax⁡\log T_{\max}logTmax​:

−H(pϕ)=∑tpϕ(t∣x)log⁡pϕ(t∣x)=∑tpϕ(t∣x)log⁡pϕ(t∣x)1/Tmax⁡−log⁡Tmax⁡=DKL(pϕ(⋅∣x)∥Uniform⁡)−log⁡Tmax⁡\begin{aligned}-H(p_\phi)&=\sum_tp_\phi(t\mid x)\log p_\phi(t\mid x)\\ &=\sum_tp_\phi(t\mid x)\log\frac{p_\phi(t\mid x)}{1/T_{\max}}-\log T_{\max}\\ &=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_\phi(\cdot\mid x)\|\operatorname{Uniform})-\log T_{\max}\end{aligned}−H(pϕ​)​=t∑​pϕ​(t∣x)logpϕ​(t∣x)=t∑​pϕ​(t∣x)log1/Tmax​pϕ​(t∣x)​−logTmax​=DKL​(pϕ​(⋅∣x)∥Uniform)−logTmax​​

So up to a constant the objective is

L=Et∼pϕ[L(t)]+βDKL(pϕ∥Uniform⁡)\begin{aligned}\mathcal L&=\mathbb E_{t\sim p_\phi}[\mathcal L^{(t)}]+\beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_\phi\|\operatorname{Uniform})\end{aligned}L​=Et∼pϕ​​[L(t)]+βDKL​(pϕ​∥Uniform)​

— the standard ELBO shape, with the exit depth as a latent variable and a uniform prior over depths. β\beta β is the usual prior weight: large β\beta β keeps the posterior spread out (exploration), small β\beta β lets it sharpen on the depth the model believes is right. The collapse described in §4.2 is exactly posterior collapse, and the entropy term is exactly the standard remedy.

A.4 Why input injection helps a data-dependent iterative solver

For a solver update wt+1=wt−η∇wE(wt,D)w_{t+1}=w_{t}-\eta \nabla _w E(w_{t},D)wt+1​=wt​−η∇w​E(wt​,D), the operator needs the data D or a sufficient representation at each step. Injection R(wt,D)R(w_{t},D)R(wt​,D) provides it directly. Without injection, an augmented state st=(wt,D)s_{t}=(w_{t},D)st​=(wt​,D) could retain D and update only w; that is a counterexample to the claim that all autonomous recurrences are incapable of data-dependent optimization.

A narrower impossibility statement is valid: if the same data-independent R is a global contraction with a unique fixed point on the entire state space, then every initialization converges to that same fixed point. Encoding different inputs only in s₀ cannot yield different limiting answers. To retain input dependence one must relax that premise, for example through input injection, preserved state coordinates, multiple attractors, finite-step readout, or external memory. The cited empirical ablations support injection as an effective design, not as a universal theorem.

BBackground concepts

Everything in this guide that is assumed rather than derived, explained from scratch. Skip what you know.

B.1 Complexity theory in fifteen minutes

The complexity results in §0 and §3 are the formal backbone of the whole subject, so they are worth actually understanding rather than nodding at.

The object: a Boolean circuit

Forget Turing machines for a moment. Picture a circuit of logic gates, with nnn input wires and one output wire. Two numbers describe it:

SizeThe number of gates. This is total work — roughly, how much silicon or how many operations.
DepthThe length of the longest path from an input to the output. This is sequential time — how many gate delays before the answer is stable, assuming every gate that can fire in parallel does.
Why this is the right model for a transformer

A transformer forward pass is a fixed computation graph: attention and MLP blocks, one after another, LLL times. Its depth is O(L)O(L)O(L) and does not grow with the input length nnn. So a fixed-depth transformer is literally a constant-depth circuit family, and the question "what can a transformer compute in one pass?" is exactly the question "what can constant-depth circuits compute?" — which complexity theorists have been answering since the 1980s.

A single circuit only handles one input size, so we talk about a circuit family: one circuit per input length nnn. That creates a loophole — you could hide an uncomputable answer in the choice of circuit for each nnn. Uniform closes the loophole: the circuit for size nnn must itself be generatable by a simple algorithm from nnn. Whenever you see "uniform TC⁰," that word is doing real work; without it the class is much bigger and the theorem would be vacuous.

The classes, from smallest up

ClassName & definitionWhat lives there / what doesn't
AC⁰ Alternating Circuit, level 0. Constant depth, polynomial size, unbounded fan-in AND / OR / NOT gates. Can do: OR of all bits, simple pattern matching. Provably cannot do PARITY (is the number of 1s odd?) — one of the few unconditional lower bounds in all of complexity theory.
TC⁰ Threshold Circuit, level 0. Same, but gates may be majority / threshold gates ("did more than kkk of my inputs fire?"). Majority makes it much stronger: integer addition, multiplication, division, sorting, matrix products — and it can do PARITY, so AC⁰ ⊊ TC⁰ is proven. This is where a log-precision transformer lives. Note that a softmax over many values is essentially a weighted threshold operation, which is why transformers land exactly here.
NC¹ Nick's Class, level 1 (after Nick Pippenger). O(log⁡n)O(\log n)O(logn) depth, polynomial size, bounded fan-in (each gate has ≤ 2 inputs). Depth now grows — slowly — with the input. Contains TC⁰. Contains iterated composition in a non-solvable group (Barrington), regular-language recognition, and evaluating Boolean formulas. TC⁰ ⊆ NC¹ is known; TC⁰ ≠ NC¹ is believed but not proven.
NC The union of all NC^k: polylogarithmic depth, polynomial size. The formal meaning of "efficiently parallelisable." A problem in NC can be solved exponentially faster with many processors than with one.
L / NL Logarithmic space, and Nondeterministic logarithmic space. Measured in memory, not time: you may only keep O(log⁡n)O(\log n)O(logn) bits of working state (a few pointers into the input). NL's signature problem is st-connectivity: is there a path from sss to ttt in a directed graph? It is NL-complete. NC¹ ⊆ L ⊆ NL.
P Polynomial time on an ordinary sequential machine. The usual informal meaning of "tractable." P-complete problems are the hardest in P and are believed inherently sequential — no parallel algorithm gives more than a polynomial speedup. Circuit-value evaluation is the classic example.
AC0⊊TC0⊆NC1⊆L⊆NL⊆PAC0⊊TC0: proven strict; PARITY separates themTC0⊆NC1: believed strict, not provenMost impossibility claims depend on longstanding conjectures.\begin{aligned}\mathrm{AC}^0&\subsetneq\mathrm{TC}^0\subseteq\mathrm{NC}^1\subseteq\mathrm L\subseteq\mathrm{NL}\subseteq\mathrm P\\ \mathrm{AC}^0\subsetneq\mathrm{TC}^0&:\ \text{proven strict; PARITY separates them}\\ \mathrm{TC}^0\subseteq\mathrm{NC}^1&:\ \text{believed strict, not proven}\\ &\text{Most impossibility claims depend on longstanding conjectures.}\end{aligned}AC0AC0⊊TC0TC0⊆NC1​⊊TC0⊆NC1⊆L⊆NL⊆P: proven strict; PARITY separates them: believed strict, not provenMost impossibility claims depend on longstanding conjectures.​

Hard, complete, and reductions

Three words that get used constantly and are easy to conflate:

  • A reduction from problem XXX to problem YYY is a translation that turns any instance of XXX into an instance of YYY with the same answer. If you can solve YYY, you can solve XXX: so YYY is at least as hard as XXX.
  • XXX is C-hard if every problem in class C reduces to XXX. So XXX is at least as hard as everything in C — but XXX need not itself be in C; it could be harder still.
  • XXX is C-complete if it is C-hard and is itself in C. It is then a "hardest representative" of C: solve it efficiently and you solve all of C efficiently.
Why the kind of reduction is always specified

The reduction must be weaker than the class you are studying, or it cheats. If you allowed polynomial-time reductions while studying P, the reduction could just solve the problem itself and every problem in P would be "complete." Hence logspace reductions for P-completeness (the translation may use only O(log⁡n)O(\log n)O(logn) memory) and even weaker AC⁰ reductions for the small circuit classes. When you read "P-complete under logspace reductions," the qualifier is what makes the statement meaningful.

Two more terms used in the text

  • Turing complete — able to simulate any computation, given unbounded time and memory. It is an expressiveness claim and says nothing about efficiency. Note that every Turing-completeness result for a neural architecture rests on idealisations (unbounded precision, unbounded steps) that real hardware violates; treat these results as "no architectural barrier," not "works in practice."
  • Chomsky hierarchy — regular ⊂ context-free ⊂ context-sensitive ⊂ recursively enumerable. A rough ladder of language-recognition power; "context-sensitive" sits roughly at "recognisable with memory proportional to the input."
What these results do and do not say

Do: for any fixed architecture there is an input size beyond which certain problems become impossible in a single forward pass, because the required sequential depth exceeds what the architecture has. That is a statement about a family of problems as n→∞n \to \infty n→∞.

Do not: say that a specific 70B model cannot add two three-digit numbers, or that it cannot answer a particular multi-hop question. Small instances need small depth, and 80 layers is a lot of depth. The theory tells you the shape of the wall, not where a given model hits it.

B.2 Mathematics used in this guide

ConceptWhat it means, and where it appears here
Fixed pointA value unchanged by the map: z∗=f(z∗)z^* = f(z^*)z∗=f(z∗). If iterating fff converges, it converges to a fixed point. §2 (DEQ), §5 (latent trajectories).
AttractorA fixed point (or cycle) that nearby trajectories fall into. "Path independence" (§2) means the same attractor is reached from different starting points.
Contraction / monotone operatorA map that pulls points closer together, guaranteeing convergence to a unique fixed point. The 1-step gradient approximation (§A.1) is only valid when the recursion is strongly contracting.
Jacobian JfJ_fJf​The matrix of all first partial derivatives of a vector-valued function — the local linear approximation of fff. Appears as ∂f∂z\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}∂z∂f​ in §A.1.
Implicit function theoremThe result licensing §A.1: if zzz is defined implicitly by an equation rather than an explicit formula, you can still differentiate it, by differentiating the equation. This is how DEQs get gradients without unrolling.
Neumann series(I−J)−1=I+J+J2+J3+…(I - J)^{-1} = I + J + J^{2} + J^{3} + \ldots (I−J)−1=I+J+J2+J3+…, valid when JJJ is small enough. Truncating after kkk terms is exactly what truncated backpropagation through kkk steps computes, and keeping only the first term (III) is the 1-step gradient. §A.1.
KL divergence KL⁡(p∥q)\operatorname{KL}(p \| q)KL(p∥q)A non-symmetric measure of how different two probability distributions are; zero exactly when they are equal. Used as the adaptive-exit criterion in Huginn (§4.1: stop when successive output distributions barely differ) and as the prior term in §A.3.
Entropy H(p)H(p)H(p)−∑xp(x)log⁡p(x)-\sum_xp(x)\log p(x)−∑x​p(x)logp(x) — how spread out a distribution is. Maximal for uniform, zero for a point mass. The entropy bonus in Ouro's objective (§4.2) is literally "keep the exit-depth distribution from collapsing to a point."
Variational inference / ELBOA family of methods that fit a distribution over an unobserved variable by maximising a lower bound on the likelihood. The bound always has the shape expected loss + KL to a prior. §A.3 shows Ouro's objective is exactly this, with exit depth as the latent variable.
Posterior collapseThe classic failure of such methods: the fitted distribution degenerates to a point and stops depending on the input. Ouro's exit gate collapsing onto Tmax⁡T_{\max}Tmax​ (§4.2) is this failure, and the entropy term is the standard remedy.
Log-normal PoissonSample a rate from a log-normal distribution, then a count from a Poisson with that rate. Gives a positive integer with a controllable mean and a heavy right tail — most steps cheap, occasional steps very deep. Huginn's recurrence sampler (§1.4).
PCAPrincipal Component Analysis — find the directions of greatest variance in a cloud of high-dimensional points and project onto the first few. Used in §5.1 to make 5280-dimensional latent trajectories visible in 2-D.
Logit lens / coda lensInterpretability probes: push an intermediate hidden state through the model's output head to see "what token it currently looks like." The coda lens first routes it through the coda block, which is the architecturally correct decoder for this model. §5.2 shows the two disagree violently, which is the main negative result there.
Big-O and ΩO(f)O(f)O(f) is an upper bound up to constants ("no worse than"), Ω(f)\Omega (f)Ω(f) a lower bound ("at least"). A result stated with Ω\Omega Ω is a hardness claim: §3.4's "requires Ω(N) bits of state" means no design can do better.

CGlossary

ACTAdaptive Computation Time. Per-token learned halting via accumulated halting probabilities plus a ponder cost (§A.2).
CodaThe non-recurrent output block that decodes the final latent state into logits. Opposite of prelude.
Coda lensDecoding an intermediate hidden state by routing it through the coda block before the output head — the architecturally correct alternative to the logit lens for a prelude/core/coda model.
Deep supervisionApplying the loss at multiple points in the recursion, usually with the state detached between segments. Bounds memory and makes intermediate states valid answers.
DEQDeep Equilibrium Model. Solves directly for the fixed point z∗=f(z∗,x)z^* = f(z^*, x)z∗=f(z∗,x); gradients by implicit differentiation with O(1)O(1)O(1) memory.
Effective depthD=k⋅LD = k\cdot LD=k⋅L: layers in the loop block times iterations. The number of sequential transformations actually applied.
Input injectionRe-feeding the embedded input at every iteration: st=R(st−1,e)s_{t} = R(s_{t-1}, e)st​=R(st−1​,e). Load-bearing (§A.4). Called "recall" in the deep-thinking literature.
Iso-FLOP baseline(kL⊗1)(kL \otimes 1)(kL⊗1) — same compute and depth as the looped model, but LLL× the parameters. The hard comparison.
Iso-param baseline(k⊗1)(k \otimes 1)(k⊗1) — same parameters, LLL× less compute. The easy comparison.
Latent thoughtOne iteration's worth of update to the latent state at one position. A loop over nnn positions produces nnn latent thoughts per iteration, versus one thought token per CoT step.
Logit lensProjecting an intermediate hidden state directly through the output embedding to see "what token it looks like." Assumes vocabulary alignment, which a loop has no reason to maintain (§5.2).
LoopLMOuro's term for a looped language model — a shared stack applied TTT times with a learned exit gate.
Middle loopingKeeping distinct layers at the start and end and looping only the middle block. Usually better than looping everything.
OverthinkingDegradation when a recurrent model is run for many more iterations than it was trained with. Input injection and randomized iteration counts mitigate it in studied settings; they do not guarantee its absence.
Path independenceConverging to the same attractor regardless of initialisation. Causally linked to benefiting from extra test-time compute (§2).
PreludeThe non-recurrent input block that embeds tokens into the latent space the loop operates in.
Truncated BPTTBackpropagating through only the last kkk iterations. Makes memory independent of rrr; keeps the first kkk terms of the Neumann series for the exact gradient.
UpcyclingInitialising a larger shared block by duplicating a smaller trained model's layers, then continuing pre-training.
Continuous depth batchingScheduling tokens by loop step rather than by forward pass, so a token on its first pass and one on its fourth share a batch. Possible only because every depth uses the same weights. §7.3.
Refill modeFilling the slots freed by early-exiting tokens with new tokens mid-pass. Necessary below B∗B^*B∗, where a shrinking batch saves FLOPs but not wall-clock time. §7.3.
Last-exited cacheCopy-on-exit: when a token exits at depth rtr_trt​, its final state is copied into the KV slots for the steps it skipped, so deeper tokens always find an entry to attend to. §7.2.
Recursion-wise cachingOne KV cache per loop step, holding entries only for tokens still active at that depth — so the cache shrinks as tokens exit. §7.2.
Cross-loop KV reuseReusing the first loop's key/value entries at later depths. Sound without any training because every loop applies the same WK,WVW_K, W_VWK​,WV​. §7.2.
Saturation batch B∗B^*B∗The batch size at which decode stops being memory-bound. Roughly rrr× smaller for a looped model than a dense one of equal depth, and it falls as context grows. §7.1.
Self-speculative decodingDrafting with a shallow loop count and verifying with a deep one — same weights, no draft model. Looped models get it for free. §7.4.
k⊗Lk \otimes Lk⊗LA kkk-layer block looped LLL times.

DCheck yourself

If you can answer these without looking, you have the material.

1. A colleague says "looping is just chain-of-thought in latent space, so it should strictly dominate." What's wrong?

It conflates two different resources. Both add serial depth, but CoT also creates a growing scratchpad — the emitted tokens stay in context and can be attended to later — while a compressed loop's state is bounded by the architecture forever. This is a real complexity-theoretic separation: a compressed loop stays a small-space reasoner however long it runs and (under standard assumptions) cannot decide problems that polynomial-length CoT can. Loops win on parallelism; CoT wins on memory and on stochastic branching. See §0.3.

2. You train a looped model and validation loss looks great. What's the one diagnostic you must run before believing it?

Validation perplexity as a function of rrr. Huginn's two failed runs trained to perfectly healthy-looking loss curves but scored identically at r=1r = 1r=1 and r=32r = 32r=32 — the model had learned to ignore the incoming state, making it a non-recurrent model in a recurrent wrapper. A loss curve cannot detect this; a depth sweep can. Secondarily, run the path-independence check from §2: two different random s0s_{0}s0​, same input, do the trajectories converge?

3. Why does a looped LM have worse perplexity than its iso-FLOP baseline but better reasoning?

Perplexity is driven strongly by parameter count — most of next-token prediction is memorisation and distributional fitting, and the iso-FLOP baseline has LLL× more parameters. Reasoning is driven by effective depth, which the two share. So on memorisation-flavoured metrics the baseline wins and on reasoning-flavoured ones the looped model matches or exceeds it. Ouro's controlled experiments give the mechanism directly: recurrence leaves raw knowledge storage unchanged at ~2 bits/parameter but sharply improves knowledge manipulation. §3.3, §4.2.

4. Why does input injection help, and what is the precise limitation of an autonomous recurrence?

Injection supplies the input to each update, allowing a solver such as w←w−η∇E(w,D)w\leftarrow w-\eta \nabla E(w,D)w←w−η∇E(w,D) to access D directly. An autonomous recurrence can also retain D in an augmented state, so injection is not universally necessary. The valid impossibility statement is narrower: the same globally contractive data-independent operator has one fixed point, so its limiting state cannot distinguish inputs encoded only by initialization. The cited no-injection failure is an empirical ablation of a particular recipe. §1.3, §A.4.

5. A learned gate always exits at the maximum depth. What should be checked?

Deeper exits may have lower loss, and coupled gate/model training can reinforce that preference. Entropy regularization spreads probability but does not by itself price computation: minimizing expected loss minus βH(p) gives p proportional to exp(−loss/β). Adding a depth cost λc changes this to exp[−(loss+λc)/β], or use a deliberately chosen prior. Check loss by depth, the exact gate distribution, gradient flow, and the accuracy–compute frontier before treating maximum-depth concentration as a training failure. §4.2.

6. What does early exit leave missing in a depth-indexed KV cache?

If an earlier token stops at depth 8, its depth 9–20 KV values were never computed. Reusing its deepest available entry is an approximation: tied K,V projection matrices still receive different hidden states at different depths. Sharing weights guarantees common shapes and coordinates, not identical values. A deployment must specify substitution, recomputation, training, or a redesigned cache architecture, and measure the resulting quality. §1.5.

7. Probing a depth-recurrent model with the logit lens shows no readable intermediate reasoning. Does that mean it isn't reasoning?

No — it means the intermediate states are not vocabulary-aligned. The logit lens assumes hidden states live in a basis the output head can read; a loop's intermediate states only need to be readable by the next iteration of itself. Evidence for real structured computation exists independently (fixed points, orbits, drift/sliders in PCA-projected trajectories). Equally, the negative result is not nothing: the same state decodes to numerals under one lens and to unrelated words under another, so any single-lens claim about "latent CoT" is unreliable. §5.

8. How can an existing checkpoint test a looping-inspired training bias?

The block-similarity regularizer studied by Saunshi et al. pulls groups of layer weights toward their mean during continued training. It preserves the untied architecture and does not reduce its parameter storage by itself. The reported reasoning and perplexity results motivate a controlled experiment; they do not guarantee neutral perplexity or transfer to every checkpoint. Tune its coefficient against task loss and compare matched data and compute budgets. §3.3, §7.3.

9. Which conditions can make recurrence a poor deployment choice?

At a fixed achieved quality, compare total FLOPs, sequential latency, stored weights, actual HBM traffic, KV memory, and training data. A looped model can fit in less parameter memory while requiring many block applications. If the core is reloaded each iteration, weight traffic also repeats. These costs can outweigh capacity gains on a compute-saturated or strict-latency workload, but no single bottleneck universally rules out recurrence: the relevant alternative may need different width, depth, or tensor parallelism to reach the same quality. §1.6, §7.

10. When is a one-step gradient a reasonable approximation to an equilibrium gradient?

At a differentiable fixed point, the exact sensitivity includes (I−J)−1(I-J)^{-1}(I−J)−1. If the spectral radius is below one and a suitable operator norm is small, its Neumann expansion starts I+J+J2+…I+J+J^{2}+\ldots I+J+J2+…; keeping only I drops all feedback terms. A fixed point alone does not justify the drop: J=0.9 gives inverse factor 10 instead of 1. Finite unrolling has different Jacobians along the trajectory; its gradient corresponds to a truncated Neumann series only under the relevant local fixed-point approximation. HRM/TRM benchmark changes must be interpreted with their full ablations, not assigned to this algebra alone. §A.1, §6.2.

11. Does tying the recurrent core guarantee r-fold less HBM weight traffic?

No. It guarantees fewer distinct parameters: storage is b(N0+Nr)b(N_{0}+N_{r})b(N0​+Nr​). If each loop reloads the core, step traffic is b(N0+rNr)b(N_{0}+rN_{r})b(N0​+rNr​). Ideal core residency could reduce that to b(N0+Nr)b(N_{0}+N_{r})b(N0​+Nr​), but requires a memory hierarchy and schedule that keep the core at the relevant level. A Huginn-scale 3 GB BF16 core does not fit into ordinary GPU on-chip caches. Thus the approximately 14× batch-one intensity gain and proportionally smaller saturation batch do not follow from tying alone. The benefit must be established by measured traffic. §7.1.

12. Why can early exit reduce total FLOPs without reducing a whole batch’s wall time?

If each remaining core invocation costs nearly the same weight-read time and the batch retains one token to maximum depth, removing other tokens lowers work without removing those invocations. Earlier-finishing requests may still see lower individual latency. Refilling compatible slots can improve utilization when independent ready work exists; the next dependent token of a still-running request is not yet available. Compute-bound stages, cache traffic, padding, and compaction may produce different behavior, so profile rather than infer from one saturation number. §7.3.

13. How do nonrecurrent work and the exit-depth distribution bound early-exit savings?

The ideal work ratio is F0+rmax⁡FrF0+E[d]Fr\frac{F_0+r_{\max}F_r}{F_0+\mathbb E[d]F_r}F0​+E[d]Fr​F0​+rmax​Fr​​, at most rmax⁡E[d]\frac{r_{\max}}{\mathbb E[d]}E[d]rmax​​. For F₀=4, Fᵣ=3, maximum depth 32 and mean depth 12, the ratio is 100/40=2.5×. Parameter counts alone do not determine F₀/Fᵣ, and one fewer loop is a smaller fraction of a 32-loop workload than of a four-loop workload even with no prelude overhead. Cross-model claims additionally need matched exit quality, kernels, batch scheduling, and task difficulty. §7.3.

14. What does weight sharing save in self-speculation, and what still needs measurement?

Shallow and deep execution share a checkpoint, so a separate full draft model may be unnecessary. Draft execution, branch KV, verification, and rejection correction still consume resources. Acceptance for a one-token exact proposal is 1−TV⁡(ptarget,pdraft)1-\operatorname{TV}(p_{\mathrm{target}},p_{\mathrm{draft}})1−TV(ptarget​,pdraft​); tied weights do not bound that distance. The reported LoopSpec maximum is evidence for its tested configurations, not a guarantee for all depths and loads. Enable speculation where expected accepted progress exceeds incremental cost, and preserve the chosen target distribution through the actual verifier and cache policy. §7.4.

15. Which cache strategies reduce depth-indexed memory, and which are exact?

Cross-loop substitution can reuse one set of KV entries without additional training, but generally approximates full depth-indexed attention. Copy-on-exit or recursion-wise allocation avoids entries for inactive tokens while memory can still scale with the active depth distribution. Learned latent compression or a recurrent memory architecture changes the representation and requires its own training and quality evidence. Constant storage, zero training, and exact equivalence are separate claims; shared projection matrices alone establish none of them simultaneously. §7.2.
